The chapter's first part, about eighty-some verses, was revealed when the Christians of Najran came to the city of the Prophet (ﷺ) to debate him concerning Jesus, peace be upon him.

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾: The discussion of the disjointed letters (ḥurūf al-hijā', the letters of the alphabet used as openers of some surahs) has already preceded. The majority of reciters pronounce the letter *mīm* here with a *fatḥa* when connecting the words, because two consecutive sukūns meet, as in *min al-nās*. Al-Zamakhsharī said that the vowel is the vowel of the hamza, transferred to the *mīm*. This view is weak, because it is an alif of connection (alif al-waṣl, the alif that is dropped in connected speech).

﴿The Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾: This is a refutation of the Christians in their claim that Jesus is God, because they assert that he was crucified. Thus he is not living, and he is not self-subsisting.

﴿The Book﴾: Here it refers to the Qur'an.

﴿With truth﴾: That is, it contains truth in its reports, its rulings and other matters; or, it is with entitlement (al-istiḥqāq).

﴿Confirming﴾: This has already been discussed under *muṣaddiqan limā ma'akum* (confirming what is with you).

﴿Before it﴾: The earlier books.

﴿The Torah and the Gospel﴾: These are two non-Arabic words, so what the grammarians have mentioned about their derivation and their morphological pattern is not sound.

﴿And He sent down the Criterion﴾: This means the Qur'an. It is mentioned again only to describe it as that which distinguishes between truth and falsehood. It is possible that it was mentioned first to affirm its revelation, as in His saying *muṣaddiqan limā bayna* (confirming what lies between), and then mentioned a second time to express gratitude for the guidance through it, just as He said about the Torah and the Gospel *hudan lil-nās* (guidance for mankind). It is as if He had said: "And He sent down the Criterion as guidance for mankind," and then that was omitted because the first mention of guidance indicates it. Since the intention of the speech differs in the two places, this is not repetition. It has also been said that the Criterion here is everything that distinguishes between truth and falsehood, whether a book or otherwise. It has also been said that it is the Psalms (al-Zabūr), but this is far-fetched.

﴿Nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Him﴾: This is a report about God's knowledge encompassing all things in detail. This is an attribute that Jesus did not have, nor anyone else, and so this is a refutation of the Christians.

﴿It is He who shapes you in the wombs﴾: This is a proof of the aforementioned knowledge of God. It also contains a refutation of the Christians, because Jesus could not form others; rather, he was himself formed like the rest of the children of Adam.

﴿However He wills﴾: [He shapes you] with regard to height and shortness, beauty and ugliness, colour, and other things.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verse 7–9:

﴿Among it are verses that are decisive (muhkamat)﴾ The muhkam (decisive) in the Qur'an is that whose meaning is clear and whose ruling is fixed. The mutashabih (ambiguous) is that which requires interpretation (ta'wil), or whose meaning is obscure, such as the disjointed letters (huruf al-hija'). Ibn 'Abbas said: "The muhkamat are the abrogating verses (al-nasikhat), the lawful and the unlawful; and the mutashabihat are the abrogated verses (al-mansukhat), the preceding and the succeeding (al-muqaddam wa'l-mu'akhkhar)." This is an illustration of what we have said. ﴿They are the mother of the Book﴾, that is, the foundation of its contents and the bulk of it. ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation (zaygh)﴾: it was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran, for they said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Does not your Book state that 'Isa is the Word of God and a spirit from Him?" He said: "Yes." They said: "Then that is sufficient for us." This is from the mutashabih, which they followed. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab the Jew and his brother Huyayy. Then, everyone who is an unbeliever or an innovator, or an ignorant person who follows the mutashabih of the Qur'an, is included in this. ﴿Seeking discord (ibtigha' al-fitna)﴾, that is, that they may cause people to be led astray by it. ﴿And seeking its interpretation (ta'wil)﴾, that is: they seek to interpret it according to what their doctrines require, or they seek to reach through knowledge of its interpretation what no created being can reach. ﴿And none knows its interpretation except God﴾: this is a statement that God alone knows the interpretation of the mutashabih of the Qur'an, and a rebuke of those who seek knowledge of it from people. ﴿And those firm in knowledge (al-rasikhun fi'l-'ilm)﴾ is a new sentence (mubtada') cut off from what precedes it, and the meaning is that the firm in knowledge do not know the interpretation of the mutashabih; rather they say: "We believe in it," in a manner of submission, compliance, and acknowledgment of their inability to know it. It was also said that it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to what precedes it, and that the meaning is that they know its interpretation. Both opinions are narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. The first opinion is that of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, 'A'isha, and 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, and it is the more preferred (arjah). Ibn 'Atiyya said: the mutashabih is of two kinds: a kind whose knowledge God has kept to Himself alone, and a kind which creation can reach. Thus al-rasikhun are a new sentence with regard to the first, and conjoined with regard to the second. ﴿Each is from our Lord﴾, that is: the decisive and the ambiguous are both from God. ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate﴾: this is related as the speech of the firm in knowledge, and it is possible that it is cut off, by way of instruction; the first is more preferred because of the continuity of the discourse. As for His words: ﴿And none will be reminded except the people of understanding (ulu'l-albab)﴾: this is from the speech of God Most High, not a report of the words of the firm in knowledge. ﴿Indeed, God does not fail in His promise﴾: an argument for the resurrection (ba'th); it is possible that it is part of the speech of the firm in knowledge, or that it is cut off, in which case it is the speech of God.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 11–12:

﴿Ka-da'b﴾ (kada'b) is in the nominative position, meaning: the case of these people is like the case of ﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾, and this carries a threat. ﴿And those before them﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) on "the people of Pharaoh", and by them are meant the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd and others. The pronoun refers back to the people of Pharaoh. ﴿Our signs﴾: the proofs (al-barāhīn) or the Book. ﴿You will be overcome and gathered﴾ was recited with the second-person ta' (addressing the Jews of Madina), and it was said (it refers) to the disbelievers of Quraysh. It was also recited with the ya' (third person), as a report about the Jews of Madina, and it was said: about Quraysh. It is true under every opinion. As for the Jews, they were overcome on the day of Qurayẓa, al-Naḍīr and Qaynuqāʿ. As for Quraysh, it was at Badr and other battles. The most well-known view is that it refers to Banū Qaynuqāʿ, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invited them to Islam after the battle of Badr, and they said to him: "Do not let it deceive you that you killed some men of Quraysh who did not know how to fight; if you had fought us you would have known that we are the (real) people." So the verse was revealed. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) expelled them from Madina.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 11–12:

﴿Ka-da'b﴾ (kada'b) is in the nominative position, meaning: the case of these people is like the case of ﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾, and this carries a threat. ﴿And those before them﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) on "the people of Pharaoh", and by them are meant the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd and others. The pronoun refers back to the people of Pharaoh. ﴿Our signs﴾: the proofs (al-barāhīn) or the Book. ﴿You will be overcome and gathered﴾ was recited with the second-person ta' (addressing the Jews of Madina), and it was said (it refers) to the disbelievers of Quraysh. It was also recited with the ya' (third person), as a report about the Jews of Madina, and it was said: about Quraysh. It is true under every opinion. As for the Jews, they were overcome on the day of Qurayẓa, al-Naḍīr and Qaynuqāʿ. As for Quraysh, it was at Badr and other battles. The most well-known view is that it refers to Banū Qaynuqāʿ, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invited them to Islam after the battle of Badr, and they said to him: "Do not let it deceive you that you killed some men of Quraysh who did not know how to fight; if you had fought us you would have known that we are the (real) people." So the verse was revealed. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) expelled them from Madina.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 3, verse 13:

﴿There has been a sign for you﴾. It is said that this is addressed to the believers. It is also said that it is addressed to the Jews, and that it is addressed to the Quraysh. The first view is the more likely, that it refers to the Banu Qaynuqa', to whom it was said: "You will be overcome." In it there is a threat to them and a lesson, as happened to others. ﴿In two hosts that met: one host﴾ are the Muslims and the polytheists on the Day of Badr. ﴿Seeing them as twice their number﴾. It is read as "tarawnahum" (you see them) with the ta', addressing those who were addressed by His words "there has been a sign for you." The meaning is: you see the disbelievers as twice the number of the believers. But God strengthened the Muslims with His help in proportion to their number. It is also read with the ya' (yarawnahum). In this reading the subject of "yarawnahum" is the believers, and the object is the polytheists. The pronoun in "mithlayhim" (their two times) refers to the believers, and the meaning follows what has been stated.

If it is objected that the disbelievers were more numerous than the Muslims on the Day of Badr, the answer is in two respects. The first: the disbelievers were three times the believers, since the disbelievers were nearly a thousand and the believers were three hundred and thirteen. Then God made the number of the disbelievers appear small in the eyes of the believers, until they thought that they were twice their number, so that they would be bold in fighting them, when it became clear to them that they were in accordance with what they had been informed of concerning one fighting two, from His words: ﴿If there are among you a hundred steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾ [al-Anfal: 66]. This meaning agrees with His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when He showed them to you as few when you met them, and He made you appear few in their eyes﴾ [al-Anfal: 44].

The second: some of the disbelievers withdrew, until there remained of them six hundred and twenty-six men, which was about twice the number of the Muslims.

It is also said: the subject of "yarawnahum" is a pronoun for the polytheists, and the object is a pronoun for the believers. The pronoun in "mithlayhim" may refer to the believers, and the object is the polytheists. The meaning according to this is that God made the number of the Muslims appear great in the eyes of the polytheists, until the disbelievers reckoned the believers as twice the disbelievers, or twice the believers, and they were fewer than that. God only made them appear many in their eyes so that they would be terrified of them. The words of God, exalted is He, "and He makes you appear few in their eyes," refute this view.

﴿With their own eyes﴾: "ra'ya al-'ayn" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (al-maṣdariyya, i.e., an absolute object expressing the manner of the verb), and its meaning is a clear observation about which there is no doubt.

﴿And God strengthens with His help whom He wills﴾: that is, victory is by the will of God, neither by fewness nor by multitude. For the host of the Muslims overcame the host of the disbelievers, although the disbelievers were more numerous than them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verse 14:

﴿Adorned for mankind﴾ It is said: the one who adorns is God, and it is said: the Shaytan (Satan). There is no contradiction between them: God's adornment is by bringing things into existence and preparing them for benefit, and by creating the natural disposition (jibillah) inclined toward worldly life; the Shaytan's adornment is by whispering (waswasah) and deception. ﴿And the heaped-up piles﴾ is the plural of qintar (qanatir), which is one thousand and two hundred ounces (uqiyyah). It is also said to be one thousand and two hundred mithqal, and both views are related from the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿Muqantarah (heaped-up)﴾ is formed from the word qanatir and for emphasis, like their saying "alf mu'allafah" (thousands upon thousands). It is also said: it means coined gold dinars or silver dirhams. ﴿Musawwamah (branded/grazing)﴾ means grazing, from their saying: "sama al-faras" and other animals when they roam in the pastures. It is also said: marked on their faces with marks, so it derives from the word simat, meaning signs. It is also said: prepared for jihad. ﴿That is the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾ is a belittling of it, so that people may be discouraged from it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 15–17:

﴿Say, "Shall I inform you of something better than that?"﴾ This is a preference of the Hereafter over this world, in order to encourage desire for it. The completion of the sentence is at His words: ﴿than that﴾. Then He began His words: ﴿For those who are mindful of God﴾ as an explanation of that. So "gardens" here is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is "for those who are mindful of God." It is also said that His words "for those who are mindful of God" are connected to what comes before. The completion of the sentence is at His words: "with their Lord," so "gardens" here is the predicate of an implied subject. ﴿And approval from God﴾ is an addition to the bliss of Paradise, and it is greater than the bliss, as is related in the hadith. ﴿Those who say﴾ is a description (na't) of "those who are mindful of God," and it is in the nominative case by virtue of being the subject, or in the accusative case by virtue of an implied verb. ﴿The truthful﴾ in statements and actions. ﴿The obedient﴾ meaning those who worship and obey. ﴿And those who seek forgiveness﴾: seeking forgiveness (istighfar) is asking for forgiveness. It was said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "How should we seek forgiveness?" He said: "Say, 'O God, forgive us and have mercy on us and turn to us in repentance, for You are the Ever-Returning, the Most Merciful.'"

﴿At dawn﴾: plural of sahar, which is the last part of the night. It is said that it is the last third of the night, and it is the time in which it is related that God says: "Whoever seeks forgiveness from Me, I will forgive him."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verse 18:

﴿Allah bears witness﴾ (the verse): It is a testimony from Allah, glorified is He, to Himself of His oneness. It is also said that its meaning is His informing His servants of that. ﴿And the angels and those of knowledge﴾ is a conjunction upon the Name of Allah, meaning they are witnesses to His oneness. By "those of knowledge" is meant the knowers of Allah, who establish the proofs of His oneness. ﴿Standing firm in justice﴾: "qa'iman" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the Name of Allah, or of "Huwa" (He), or it is in the accusative by way of praise (madh). ﴿In justice﴾: with equity. ﴿There is no god but He﴾: He repeated the declaration of oneness (tahlil) for two reasons. The first: He mentioned the testimony to oneness first, then mentioned it again after its establishment by the earlier testimony. The second: that is a teaching for His servants so that they would increase in saying it.

﴿Indeed, the religion [with God] is Islam﴾. It is read with a kasra on the hamza (إِنَّ) as a new sentence, and with a fatha (أَنَّ) as a *badal* (substitution, or apposition, a construction in which a noun is restated by another noun that refers to the same thing). The latter is a *badal shay' min shay'* (a substitution of a thing for a thing), because monotheism (*tawhid*) is Islam.

﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, out of rivalry between themselves﴾: this is an announcement that they differed after they had come to know the realities, out of *baghy* (transgression), which is envy. The verse concerns the Jews, and it is said that it concerns the Christians, and it is said that it concerns both.

﴿Swift in reckoning﴾: its meaning has already been explained in *al-Baqarah*. Here it is a threat, and for this reason it comes as a reply to whoever disbelieves.

﴿But if they argue with you﴾, that is, dispute with you concerning the religion. The pronoun refers to the Jews and the Christians of Najran.

﴿Then say: I have submitted my face﴾, that is, I have devoted myself and my whole being ﴿to God﴾. He expressed it by "face" as a way of referring to the whole person.

The meaning of the verse is the establishment of the proof against them, because whoever submits his face to God is undoubtedly upon the truth, so the argument of whoever opposes him falls away.

﴿And those who follow me﴾ is conjoined (*'atf*) to the *ta'* in *aslamtu* (I have submitted). It may also be an object of accompaniment (*maf'ul ma'ahu*).

﴿Have you submitted?﴾ is an affirmation (*taqrir*) after the establishment of the proof against them, meaning: proofs have already come to you that require you to submit.

﴿So upon you is only the delivering [of the message]﴾, that is, upon you is only to convey the message of your Lord. When you have conveyed it, you have done what is incumbent upon you. It is said that this contains a truce (*muwada'ah*) which was abrogated (*nasakhat*, i.e., abrogation, the replacement of a ruling by a later one) by the verse of the sword (*ayat al-sayf*, the verses commanding fighting against the disbelievers).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 21–25:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾, etc. This was revealed concerning the Jews and Christians, as a rebuke to them and a warning about the wickedness of their deeds and the deeds of their predecessors. ﴿Those who were given the Book﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 19] are the Jews, and "the Book" here is the Torah, or it refers to the category of scripture in general. ﴿They invite to the Fire, while Allah...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221]. Ibn ʿAbbās said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon a group of Jews, among whom were al-Nuʿmān ibn ʿAmr and al-Ḥārith ibn Zayd. They said to him: "On what religion are you?" He said to them: "On the religion of Ibrāhīm." They said: "Ibrāhīm was a Jew." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "Come then to the Torah; it is between us and you." They refused, and so the verse was revealed. According to this, the "Book of Allah" is the Torah. It was also said that it is the Qur'an: the Prophet (ﷺ) used to invite them to it, and they turned away from it. ﴿That is because they...﴾: the "that" refers to their turning away from the Book of Allah, and the "bāʾ" (because) is causal. The meaning is that their disbelief is due to their obstinacy and their falsehoods. The "numbered days" have been mentioned in al-Baqarah. ﴿So how will it be when We gather them﴾: that is, how will their condition be on the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is an expression of awe and magnification of what has been prepared for them.

"Allāhumma" is a vocative (munādā). According to the Basran grammarians, the mīm in it is a substitute for the vocative particle (ḥarf al-nidā'), which is why the two cannot be combined. The Kufans said its original form is "yā Allāh, ummanā bi-khayr," so the mīm, according to them, comes from "ummanā."

﴿Owner of sovereignty﴾ (mālika al-mulk) is a vocative according to Sībawayh. Al-Zajjāj permitted it to be an attributive adjective (ṣifa) of the name Allah.

It was also said that the verse was revealed as a refutation of the Christians in their claim that Jesus is God, "because these attributes do not belong to Jesus."

It was also said that when the Prophet (ﷺ) informed them that his community would conquer the realms of Kisrā and Caesar, the hypocrites found this far-fetched, and so the verse was revealed.

﴿In Your hand is the good﴾ (biyadika al-khayr). It was said: the intended meaning is "in Your hand is the good and the evil," and one of them was omitted because the other indicates it. It was also said: the good was singled out for mention because the verse carries the sense of supplication and desire, as if he were saying: "In Your hand is the good, so grant me abundantly of it."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verse 27:

﴿And You bring the living out of the dead, and You bring the dead out of the living﴾ Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: It is the sperm-drop that comes out of a man dead while he is alive, and a man comes out of it alive while it is dead. Ikrimah said: It is the bringing out of the chick from the egg, and the egg from the chick. It was also said: the disbeliever is brought out of the believer and the believer out of the disbeliever; so life and death on this view are a metaphor (isti'arah). In mentioning "the living" from "the dead" there is antithesis (mutabaqah), which is one of the tools of eloquence (adawat al-bayan). In it there is also inversion (qalb), because he placed "the living" before "the dead," and then reversed the order. ﴿Without reckoning﴾: without restriction (bi-ghayr tadyiq). It was also said: without being called to account (bi-ghayr muhasabah).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 28–31:

﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers﴾, etc. It is general for all eras. Its occasion was the inclination of some of the Ansar toward some of the Jews. It is also said: it was the letter of Hatib to the polytheists of Quraysh. ﴿Then there is nothing from Allah in anything﴾: a disavowal of whoever does that, and a warning against allying with the disbelievers. In the speech there is an ellipsis, its estimate being: "there is nothing of drawing near to Allah in anything." The position of "in anything" is accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl) clause referring to the pronoun in "from Allah," as Ibn ʿAṭiyya said. ﴿Except when you fear a danger from them﴾: a permission for alliance with them if they fear from them, and what is meant is alliance outwardly with inward hatred. ﴿Taqiyyah﴾: its pattern is fuʿlah, with the fāʾ vowelled with ḍammah and the ʿayn with fatḥah. Its fāʾ is a wāw, and a tāʾ has been substituted for it; its lām is a yāʾ, from which an alif has been substituted. ﴿Indeed, Allah chose﴾ the verse: when the discussion with the Christians of Najran had passed its opening stage, he began to explain to them what they had disagreed about and what had become unclear to them concerning the matter of Jesus, peace be upon him, and how he was born. He began with the mention of Adam and Noah, peace be upon them both, to complete the matter, since they are the two fathers of all the prophets. Then he mentioned Abraham, moving gradually toward mention of Imran, the father of Mary, the mother of Jesus, peace be upon him. It is also said that Imran here is the father of Moses, and between them there are one thousand eight hundred years. The more apparent view is that the intended Imran here is the father of Mary, because her story is mentioned after this.

﴿and the family of Abraham and the family of Imran﴾: the word "family" (āl) may mean kinsfolk or followers. On either meaning, our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is included among the family of Abraham.

﴿offspring﴾: it is either a substitute for what preceded or a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). Its form is fu‘layyah, a relative noun derived from dharr, meaning ants, because Allah brought forth creation from the loins of Adam like dharr (tiny particles).

﴿when the wife of Imran said﴾: the governing element (al-‘āmil) of this is omitted, its estimated meaning being "remember." It is also said that it is "knowing." Al-Zajjaj said that its governing element is the meaning of choosing.

﴿the wife of Imran﴾: her name was Ḥannah, with an "n," and she was the mother of Mary. This Imran is the father of Mary.

﴿I have vowed﴾: that is, I have made it a vow upon myself that this child in my womb will be dedicated to the service of Your house, which is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).

﴿dedicated﴾: that is, freed (‘atīq) from every occupation except serving the mosque.

﴿Then when she had given birth to her﴾: the verse. They did not dedicate females to serve the mosques, so she said, ﴿Indeed, I have given birth to a female﴾, in sorrow and regret over what she had lost of the vow she had made.

﴿And Allah knows best what she had given birth to﴾: it is recited as "wa-ḍa‘at" with a sukun on the tā’, and in that reading it is the speech of Allah, magnifying her giving birth. It is also recited with a ḍammah on the tā’ and a sukun on the ‘ayn, and on this reading it is the speech of the two of them.

﴿And the male is not like the female﴾: this may be the speech of Allah, meaning the male you asked for is not like the female who was given to you. It may also be her speech, meaning the male is not like the female in serving the mosques, since males used to serve them and females did not.

﴿I have named her Mary﴾: she said to her Lord, "I have named her Mary," because in their language Mary means "the worshipper," and she intended by that to draw near to Allah. From this is derived the naming of a child on the day of its birth. Mary is not declined (ghayr munṣarif) because of definiteness and feminine gender, and there is also in it non-Arabic origin.

﴿And I seek refuge for her in You﴾: it is reported in a hadith: "There is no child born except that Satan pricks it the day it is born, so it cries out, screaming, except Mary and her son," based on His saying, ﴿And I seek refuge for her in You﴾, the verse.

﴿So her Lord accepted her﴾: that is, He was pleased with her for the mosque in place of a male.

﴿with a good acceptance﴾: there are two views concerning it. One is that it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used in a form other than the usual verbal noun. The other is that it is a noun for what is accepted by it, just as as-su‘ūṭ (snuff) is a noun for what is inhaled with it.

﴿and the family of Abraham and the family of Imran﴾: the word "family" (āl) may mean kinsfolk or followers. On either meaning, our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is included among the family of Abraham.

﴿offspring﴾: it is either a substitute for what preceded or a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). Its form is fu‘layyah, a relative noun derived from dharr, meaning ants, because Allah brought forth creation from the loins of Adam like dharr (tiny particles).

﴿when the wife of Imran said﴾: the governing element (al-‘āmil) of this is omitted, its estimated meaning being "remember." It is also said that it is "knowing." Al-Zajjaj said that its governing element is the meaning of choosing.

﴿the wife of Imran﴾: her name was Ḥannah, with an "n," and she was the mother of Mary. This Imran is the father of Mary.

﴿I have vowed﴾: that is, I have made it a vow upon myself that this child in my womb will be dedicated to the service of Your house, which is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).

﴿dedicated﴾: that is, freed (‘atīq) from every occupation except serving the mosque.

﴿Then when she had given birth to her﴾: the verse. They did not dedicate females to serve the mosques, so she said, ﴿Indeed, I have given birth to a female﴾, in sorrow and regret over what she had lost of the vow she had made.

﴿And Allah knows best what she had given birth to﴾: it is recited as "wa-ḍa‘at" with a sukun on the tā’, and in that reading it is the speech of Allah, magnifying her giving birth. It is also recited with a ḍammah on the tā’ and a sukun on the ‘ayn, and on this reading it is the speech of the two of them.

﴿And the male is not like the female﴾: this may be the speech of Allah, meaning the male you asked for is not like the female who was given to you. It may also be her speech, meaning the male is not like the female in serving the mosques, since males used to serve them and females did not.

﴿I have named her Mary﴾: she said to her Lord, "I have named her Mary," because in their language Mary means "the worshipper," and she intended by that to draw near to Allah. From this is derived the naming of a child on the day of its birth. Mary is not declined (ghayr munṣarif) because of definiteness and feminine gender, and there is also in it non-Arabic origin.

﴿And I seek refuge for her in You﴾: it is reported in a hadith: "There is no child born except that Satan pricks it the day it is born, so it cries out, screaming, except Mary and her son," based on His saying, ﴿And I seek refuge for her in You﴾, the verse.

﴿So her Lord accepted her﴾: that is, He was pleased with her for the mosque in place of a male.

﴿with a good acceptance﴾: there are two views concerning it. One is that it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used in a form other than the usual verbal noun. The other is that it is a noun for what is accepted by it, just as as-su‘ūṭ (snuff) is a noun for what is inhaled with it.

﴿And He caused her to grow a good growth﴾: this is an expression for a good upbringing.

﴿And Zechariah became her guardian﴾: that is, he took her into his support and care. The kāfil is the ḥāḍin (custodian). Zechariah was the husband of her maternal aunt. It is also recited as "kaffalahā" with a shaddah on the fā’, with Zechariah in the accusative, meaning Allah made him her guardian.

﴿the prayer niche (al-miḥrāb)﴾: linguistically, it means the most noble of places of assembly, and for this reason the place of the imam is called by that name. It is said that Zechariah built for her a chamber in the mosque, and this is the miḥrāb mentioned here. It is also said that the miḥrāb is the place of worship.

﴿he found with her provision﴾: he would find with her the fruits of winter in summer, and the fruits of summer in winter. It is also said that she never suckled from a breast, and Allah was providing for her.

﴿Where did this come from for you?﴾: it is an indication of place, meaning how and from where?

﴿Indeed, Allah provides﴾: it may be the speech of Mary or the speech of Allah, the Exalted.

﴿There﴾ indicates a place, though it may also be used for a time, and the time sense is the more apparent here. That is, when Zakariyya (Zechariah) saw God's favour to Maryam (Mary), he asked God for a child.

﴿The angels called out to him﴾: the verb is feminine in form out of regard for the group. It is also read as فناداه (*fanadahu*, "called out to him" with a masculine pronoun, without the feminine ta'). It is said that the one who called to him was Jibril (Gabriel) alone. The plural "angels" is used because of the way people say "so-and-so rides horses," meaning the category of horses, even if he rides only one mount.

﴿Yahya (John)﴾ is a name that God gave him before he was born. It is a name in Hebrew which coincides in derivation and form with Arabic, and it is not inflected (*la yansarif*, i.e. it does not take nunation, the diptote). If it is taken as non-Arabic in its inflection, it has two grounds for being diptote: definiteness and foreignness (*'ujma*). If it is taken as Arabic, it has two grounds: definiteness and the morphological pattern of a verb (*wazn al-fi'l*).

﴿Confirming a word from God﴾: that is, confirming and believing in Isa (Jesus), peace be upon him. Isa was called "the Word of God" because he came into being only through God's word alone, which is the saying كن (*kun*, "Be"), and not through another cause, namely a father, as with the rest of the children of Adam.

﴿And a master﴾: *sayyid* is one who rules over his people, that is, who surpasses them in nobility and excellence.

﴿And chaste (*hasur*)﴾: that is, one who does not approach women. It is said that God created him so; it is said that he restrained himself; and it is said that *hasur* means one who does not commit sins.

﴿How can I have a son?﴾ is an expression of wonder and of considering it unlikely: that he should have a child in his old age and with his wife being barren. It is said that he was ninety-nine years old and his wife was ninety-eight. He found this unlikely according to the normal course of things, although he knew God's power to do it. So he asked, knowing God's power, and found it unlikely because it is rare in the ordinary course. It is also said that he asked when he was young and was answered when he was old, and that is why he found it unlikely.

﴿Thus does God do what He wills﴾: that is, like this wondrous deed, God does what He wills. The *kaf* (in *kadhalika*, "thus") is for comparing God's wondrous acts to this deed, and the demonstrative "thus" refers to the granting of a child to Zakariyya. The word "God" is in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), and "thus" is its predicate (*khabar*), so it must be connected to it. It is also said that the predicate is "does what He wills," and on this view *kadhalika* may take two readings. One is that it is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from the agent of "does." The other is that it is in the position of the predicate of an omitted subject, with the sense "the matter is thus," or "you two are thus," and on this view one stops at *kadhalika*. The first is preferable, because the speech is connected and the phrase "does what He wills" is bound to what precedes it, and because the Qur'an has many parallels, among them the verse ﴿And such is the seizure of your Lord﴾ (Hud 11:102).

﴿Give me a sign﴾, that is, a sign of the woman's pregnancy.

﴿Your sign is that you will not speak to people﴾, that is, your sign is that you will not be able to speak to people.

﴿For three days﴾: his tongue is restrained from that, while speech is preserved in the remembrance of God. That is why He said: ﴿And remember your Lord much﴾. His tongue was restrained from speech for that period only so that in it he would devote himself purely to the remembrance of God, giving thanks for the answering of his prayer, and so that his tongue would not be occupied with anything other than thanks and remembrance.

﴿Except by signs﴾, that is, by a gesture with the hand, the head, or something else. This is an exceptional clause of the disconnected kind (*istithna' munqati'*).

﴿In the evening﴾ means from the decline of the sun to its setting, and ﴿in the morning﴾ (*al-ibkar*) means from the break of dawn to the forenoon.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verse 42:

﴿And when the angels said﴾: It is disputed whether the intended one is Gabriel or a group of angels? The governing element of "when" (idh) is an implied verb. ﴿He has chosen you﴾ first, when He accepted you from your mother, ﴿and purified you﴾ from every defect in creation, character and religion, ﴿and chosen you above the women of the worlds﴾. This choosing may be particular: that He granted her Jesus without a father, so that "above the women of the worlds" is general. Or the choosing may be general, and it specifies from among the women of the worlds Khadijah and Fatimah. Or the meaning may be: above the women of her own time. It has been said that she is preferred absolutely, and it has been said that she was a prophetess, since the angels spoke to her.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 43–48:

﴿ٱقْنُتِي﴾ Al-qunut here means obedience and worship. It was also said: prolonged standing in prayer, and this is the view of most scholars. ﴿وَٱسْجُدِي وَٱرْكَعِي﴾ She was commanded to pray, so qunut and prostration were mentioned because they are part of the form of prayer and its pillars. Then it was said to her: "Bow with those who bow," meaning: let your prayer be with those who pray, or in congregation. According to this reading, the speech does not require placing prostration before bowing, because it did not refer to bowing and prostration combined in a single rak'ah. It was also said that this is what was meant, and that prostration was mentioned first because the conjunction wa' does not indicate sequence. It is also possible that prayer in their religion had prostration before bowing.

﴿ذٰلِكَ﴾ refers to what has preceded of the narratives, and it is an address to the Prophet ﷺ. ﴿وَمَا كُنتَ لَدَيْهِمْ﴾ is an argument for his prophethood ﷺ, since he reported these accounts while he was not present with them. ﴿يُلْقُون أَقْلَٰمَهُمْ﴾ means their azlam, which are their arrows (qidah, lots). It was also said: the pens with which they used to write the Torah. They cast lots with them over the guardianship of Maryam, out of eagerness for her and rivalry over her care. The verse indicates the permissibility of drawing lots, and it has also been established in the Sunnah. ﴿أَيُّهُمْ يَكْفُلُ مَرْيَمَ﴾ is a subject and predicate in a position of accusative, governed by a verb whose implied sense is: "they look to see which of them." ﴿يَخْتَصِمُونَ﴾ means they dispute over which of them will take charge of her. ﴿إِذْ قَالَتِ ٱلْمَلاۤئِكَةُ﴾ إذ is a substitute (badal) for إذ in إذ قالت, or for إذ in إذ يختصمون, and its governing verb is implied. ﴿ٱسْمُهُ﴾ the masculine pronoun refers back to the word (kalimah), because the one named by it was mentioned. ﴿ٱلْمَسِيحُ﴾ It was said: it is derived from sahha fi al-ard (to travel in the land), so its pattern is maf'il. Most scholars said: it is from masaha (to wipe), because he was wiped with blessing, so its pattern is fa'il. He said "Isa son of Maryam" while the address is to Maryam, to attribute him to her, informing that he would be born without a father. ﴿وَجِيهاً﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). His standing (wajahah) in this world is prophethood and precedence over people; in the Hereafter it is intercession and high rank in Paradise. ﴿فِي ٱلْمَهْدِ﴾ is in a position of circumstantial state (hal). ﴿وَكَهْلاً﴾ is conjoined to it. The meaning is that he speaks to people as a child, a sign indicating the innocence of his mother from what the Jews accused her of, and indicating his prophethood. He also speaks to them as an adult, which informs of his living until he reaches the age of kuhulah (middle age). Its beginning is thirty-three years, and it was said: forty. ﴿وَيُعَلِّمُهُ﴾ is conjoined to yubashshiruki or wa-yukallimu. ﴿ٱلْكِتَٰبَ﴾ here is a genus; it was said: writing by hand. And al-hikmah here means the religious sciences, or correctness in speech and action.

It is also read with a kasra, in which case it begins a new statement. **﴿Then I breathe into it﴾**: the pronoun is masculine here because it refers to the clay (الطين), or to the kaf in كهيئة (kahay'ah, "in the form of"). Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verse 51:

﴿Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord.﴾ This is a refutation of those who attributed lordship (rububiyyah) to Jesus. The speech of Jesus, peace be upon him, ends at his words: ﴿This is a straight path.﴾ and its beginning is from his words: "Indeed, I have come to you..." All of this may be part of what the angels said to Mary, relating that Jesus, peace be upon him, would say it. It may also be that the address to Mary had ended, and then the speech resumed from his words "and a messenger," on the assumption that Jesus came as a messenger: "Indeed, I have come to you with a sign from your Lord," and then his speech continued to its end.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 52–53:

﴿When Jesus sensed disbelief from them﴾: i.e., he knew it with an apparent knowledge, like the knowledge of what is perceived by the senses. ﴿said, "Who are my helpers toward Allah?"﴾: a request for support. The word "ansar" (helpers) is the plural of "nasir" (helper). ﴿toward Allah﴾: its implied sense is, "Who will join their selves to Allah in supporting me?" Therefore it is said that "ila" here means "ma'a" (with), or that it is connected to an omitted element, meaning "going" or "seeking refuge" toward Allah. ﴿The disciples said﴾: "al-hawariyyun" (the disciples). The "hawari" of a man is his choice and close companion. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every prophet has a hawari, and my hawari is al-Zubayr." It is also said that the disciples were launderers who whitened clothes (yuhawiruna al-thiyab, i.e., they bleached them), and that is why they were called "al-hawariyyun." ﴿We believe in Allah, and bear witness that we are Muslims. ... "Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down (anzalta)"﴾: they mean the Gospel, and "the Messenger" here is Jesus, peace be upon him. ﴿and we follow the messenger, so write us among the witnesses﴾: i.e., among those who bear witness to the truth from the nations. It is also said: among the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), because they bear witness over the people.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 54–58:

﴿وَمَكَرُواْ﴾ The pronoun refers to the disbelievers among the Children of Israel, and their scheming was that they assigned someone to kill Jesus secretly (ghīlah). ﴿وَمَكَرَ ٱللَّهُ﴾ That is, He raised Jesus up to the heaven, and cast his likeness upon the one who intended to assassinate him, so that he was killed in his place. Indeed, the likeness of Jesus ﴿...﴾ is an argument against the Christians in their saying: "How can someone be born without a father?" So God made his likeness Adam, whom God created without a mother or a father, and that is more remarkable than what they found improbable, so it is a stronger refutation of their claim. ﴿He created him from dust﴾ is an explanation of Adam's condition, so it is a report about a past state. The original form would have been: "He created him from dust, then said to him 'Be,' and he was." But he placed the present tense in the position of the past tense to depict in the minds of the addressees that the matter is as if present and continuous. ﴿The truth﴾ is the predicate of an implied subject. ﴿So whoever disputes with you concerning it﴾ means concerning Jesus. Those who disputed with him about it were the delegation of Najran from the Christians, and they had two leaders, one called al-Sayyid and the other al-'Aqib. ﴿Let us invoke a curse﴾ means let us invoke mutual cursing (mula'ana). The word mubahalah (mutual imprecation) means curse, i.e., we say: "May the curse of God be upon the liar among us and you." This is the origin of ibtihal (invoking a curse), which was then used for any earnest supplication, even if it does not involve a curse. When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent for Ali, Fatimah, al-Hasan and al-Husayn, and invited the Christians of Najran to mutual cursing. They feared that God would destroy them or transform them into apes and pigs, so they refused the mutual cursing and agreed to pay the jizya (poll tax).

**﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture...﴾** This is addressed to the Christians of Najran, though it is also said to be addressed to the Jews. **﴿A word that is equitable﴾**, meaning just and fair, **﴿that we worship none but Allah﴾**. Here أَلاَّ نَعْبُدَ (*allā naʿbuda*, "that we not worship") is in apposition (بدل, *badal*) to the word *kalimah*, or it is in the nominative on the assumption of an implied هِيَ (*hiya*, "it is"). The Prophet (ﷺ) (ﷺ) called them to the Oneness of God (توحيد, *tawhid*, affirmation of God's unity) and to abandoning what they worshipped besides Him, such as al-Masih (the Messiah), the rabbis (الأحبار, *al-aḥbār*) and the monks (الرهبان, *al-ruhbān*).

**﴿Why do you argue about Abraham﴾**: The Jews said, "Abraham was a Jew," and the Christians said, "He was a Christian." So the verse was revealed as a refutation of them, because the religious community (ملة, *millah*) of the Jews and the Christians came into being only a long time after the death of Abraham.

**﴿Ha-antum﴾**: ها (*hā*) is a particle of attention-calling (تنبيه, *tanbīh*). It is also said that it replaces the interrogative hamzah. Then أنتم (*antum*, "you") is the subject (مبتدأ, *mubtadaʾ*) and هؤلاء (*hāʾulāʾ*, "these") is its predicate, and حاججتم (*ḥājajtum*, "you argued") is a resumptive new sentence (استئناف, *istiʾnāf*). Alternatively, هؤلاء is in the accusative by specification (التخصيص, *takhṣīṣ*), and حاججتم is the predicate.

**﴿About what you have knowledge of﴾**: that is, about what the Torah and the Gospel have spoken of.

**﴿About what you have no knowledge of﴾**: that is, what preceded that concerning the condition of Abraham.

**﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian﴾**: a refutation of the Jews and the Christians.

**﴿Nor was he of the polytheists﴾**: a negation of *shirk* (association of partners with God), which is the worship of idols, and this also includes the form of *shirk* contained in the religion of the Jews and the Christians.

**﴿And this Prophet﴾**: this is in coordination (عطف, *ʿaṭf*) with "those who followed him," meaning Muhammad (ﷺ) (ﷺ).

**﴿Are most worthy of Abraham among the people﴾**, because he (ﷺ) (ﷺ) follows his religion.

**﴿And those who believe﴾**: the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) (ﷺ).

So the verse was revealed as a refutation of them, because the religious community (ملة, *millah*) of the Jews and the Christians came into being only a long time after the death of Abraham.

**﴿Ha-antum﴾**: ها (*hā*) is a particle of attention-calling (تنبيه, *tanbīh*). It is also said that it replaces the interrogative hamzah. Then أنتم (*antum*, "you") is the subject (مبتدأ, *mubtadaʾ*) and هؤلاء (*hāʾulāʾ*, "these") is its predicate, and حاججتم (*ḥājajtum*, "you argued") is a resumptive new sentence (استئناف, *istiʾnāf*). Alternatively, هؤلاء is in the accusative by specification (التخصيص, *takhṣīṣ*), and حاججتم is the predicate.

**﴿About what you have knowledge of﴾**: that is, about what the Torah and the Gospel have spoken of.

**﴿About what you have no knowledge of﴾**: that is, what preceded that concerning the condition of Abraham.

**﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian﴾**: a refutation of the Jews and the Christians.

**﴿Nor was he of the polytheists﴾**: a negation of *shirk* (association of partners with God), which is the worship of idols, and this also includes the form of *shirk* contained in the religion of the Jews and the Christians.

**﴿And this Prophet﴾**: this is in coordination (عطف, *ʿaṭf*) with "those who followed him," meaning Muhammad (ﷺ) (ﷺ).

**﴿Are most worthy of Abraham among the people﴾**, because he (ﷺ) (ﷺ) follows his religion.

**﴿And those who believe﴾**: the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) (ﷺ).

A group of the People of the Book wished to lead you astray. They are the Jews, who invited Hudhayfah, 'Ammar and Mu'adh to Judaism. ﴿And they lead astray none but themselves﴾, meaning the burden of misguiding others falls back only on them. ﴿While you bear witness﴾, meaning you know that Muhammad (ﷺ) is a prophet. ﴿Why do you mix the truth with falsehood?﴾, meaning you confuse them: the truth is the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and falsehood is disbelief in him. ﴿Believe in what has been revealed﴾. A group of the Jews, may Allah curse them, outwardly embraced Islam at the beginning of the day and then disbelieved at its end, in order to deceive the Muslims, so that they would say: "These people have turned back only because they have knowledge." Al-Suhayli said that this group were 'Abd Allah ibn al-Sayf, 'Adi ibn Zayd and al-Harith ibn 'Awf. ﴿That anyone should be given the like of what you were given﴾. This may be part of the speech that the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to say, connected to his words, "Indeed, guidance is the guidance of Allah." It may also be part of the speech of the People of the Book, connected to their words, "Do not believe except in those who follow your religion." In that case, "Indeed, guidance…" is a parenthetical interjection between the two statements.

On the first reading, the meaning is: "lest anyone be given the like of what you were given," since they said what they said and plotted what they plotted of deception. The phrase "an yu'ta" (that it be given) is then the object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), or it is governed by a suppressed verb, the sense being: "Do not deny that anyone may be given the like of what you were given of the Book and prophethood."

On the second reading, the meaning is: "Do not believe, that is, do not acknowledge that anyone may be given the like of what you were given." Here the phrase "an yu'ta" is the object of "tu'minu" (believe), which is understood to include the sense of "tuqirru" (acknowledge). It is also possible that it stands in the position of the object of purpose: "Do not believe except in those who follow your religion, out of aversion that anyone be given the like of what you were given."

﴿Except to those who follow your religion﴾, and keep this concealed from those who do not follow your religion, lest they invite them to Islam.

﴿Or that they might argue with you﴾. This is coordinated with "an yu'ta" (that anyone be given). The subject pronoun refers to the Muslims, and the object pronoun refers to the Jews.

﴿Indeed, bounty is in the hand of Allah﴾. This is a rebuttal of the Jews in their claim that Allah had not given anyone the like of what He gave the Children of Israel of prophethood and nobility.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verse 75–76:

﴿وَمِنْ أَهْلِ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ﴾ [And among the People of the Book] ... the verse: an information that the People of the Books are of two kinds: trustworthy (amin), and treacherous (kha'in). He mentioned the qintar (a large weight of gold, often glossed as a great quantity of wealth) as an example of the abundant; so whoever pays it back, pays what is less than it, and he mentioned the dinar (a gold coin) as an example of the little, so whoever refuses it, refuses what is above it by way of greater priority. ﴿قَآئِماً﴾ [standing] may be understood as standing in the literal sense with the body, or as standing by the matter, meaning being resolute in it. ﴿ذٰلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمْ﴾ [That is because they...] The reference is to their treachery, and the bāʾ (ba, "because of") is for causation. ﴿لَيْسَ عَلَيْنَا﴾ [There is no blame upon us] They claimed that the wealth of the Ummiyyun, which is the Arabs, is lawful for them. ﴿ٱلْكَذِبَ﴾ [the lie] here refers to their saying that God made it lawful for them in the Torah, or their lying in general. ﴿بَلَىٰ﴾ [Yes indeed] there is a way and a due claim of responsibility over them regarding the wealth of the Ummiyyun. ﴿بِعَهْدِهِ﴾ [with His covenant] The pronoun refers either to "man" (man) or to God.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 77–78:

﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of Allah﴾ (the verse). It is said: it was revealed concerning the Jews, because they abandoned the covenant of Allah in the Torah for the sake of worldly gain. And it is said: it was revealed on account of a dispute between al-Ash'ath ibn Qays and another man, and his opponent wanted to swear falsely. ﴿And indeed among them﴾: the pronoun refers to the People of the Scripture. ﴿Who distort their tongues﴾, meaning they distort the wording or the meaning. ﴿That you may think it﴾: the pronoun refers to what is indicated by His saying "who distort their tongues," namely the distorted speech.

﴿مَا كَانَ لِبَشَرٍ﴾ (It is not for a human being) – the answer. This negation governs ﴿ثُمَّ يَقُولَ لِلنَّاسِ﴾ (then say to the people). The meaning is: no one to whom Allah has given prophethood claims divinity. The reference is to Jesus (peace be upon him), a refutation of the Christians who said he is God. It is also said to refer to Muhammad (ﷺ), because the Jews said: "O Muhammad, do you want us to worship you as the Christians worshipped Jesus?" So he said: "God forbid! That is not what I was commanded, nor to it did I call." ﴿رَبَّانِيِّينَ﴾ (rabbaniyyin, masters of the divine) is the plural of rabbani (rabbānī), meaning a scholar. It is also said that the rabbani is one who trains people by teaching them the small matters of knowledge before the great ones. ﴿بِمَا كُنتُمْ﴾ (by what you were): the bāʾ (ب) is causal (sababiyyah), and mā is verbal-masdarian (maṣdariyyah). ﴿تُعَلِّمُونَ﴾ (teaching) with light pronunciation (bi-l-takhfīf), meaning "you know" (تَعْرِفُونَ). This is the reading of Nafiʿ and others. It is also read with tashdid, from teaching (التَّعْلِيم). ﴿وَلاَ يَأْمُرَكُمْ﴾ (nor would he command you) with a raised ending (marfūʿ) is a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf), and its subject is Allah or the human being mentioned. It is also read with a fatha ending (manṣūb), coordinated either with ﴿أَن يُؤْتِيَهُ﴾ (that Allah should give him) or with ﴿ثُمَّ يَقُولَ﴾ (then say), and in this reading the subject is the human being.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 81–82:

﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets﴾. The meaning of the verse is that Allah took the pledge and covenant from every prophet that he must believe in Muhammad ﷺ and support him if he should live to see him. This includes the taking of this covenant from the nations of the prophets. The lam in His words ﴿what I have given you﴾ is the lam of preparation (lam al-tawti'ah), because the taking of a covenant carries the sense of an oath of succession. The lam in ﴿you will surely believe in him﴾ is the answer to the oath, and "ma" may be conditional, so that ﴿you will surely believe﴾ stands in the place of the answer to both the oath and the condition. It may also be relative, meaning "that which We have given you." ﴿You will surely believe in him﴾: the pronoun in "him" refers to the Messenger. ﴿And you will surely support him﴾. ﴿Do you acknowledge﴾, i.e., do you confess ﴿My covenant﴾, i.e., My pledge? ﴿Then bear witness﴾, i.e., against yourselves and against your nations, by your commitment to this covenant. ﴿And I am with you﴾ is a confirmation of the covenant by the witness of the Lord of Might, majestic is His majesty. ﴿After that﴾, i.e., whoever turns away from faith in this Prophet ﷺ after this covenant, he is a defiant, rebellious apostate in his disbelief.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary on Surah 3, verse 83 (al-Tashil)

﴿أَفَغَيْرَ﴾ The hamza is for rebuke (al-inkar), and the fa' (fa) conjoins one sentence to another. Ghayr (other than) is the object, placed first for emphasis on it or for restriction (al-hasr).

﴿وَلَهُ أَسْلَمَ﴾ That is, submitted and surrendered (inqada wa-istaslama).

﴿طَوْعاً وَكَرْهاً﴾ These are verbal nouns (masdar) placed in the position of a circumstantial state (hal). Willing submission (al-taw') belongs to the believers, and unwilling submission (al-kurh) to the disbeliever when he witnesses death. It was also said: at the taking of the earlier covenant (akhdh al-mithaq). And it was said: the acknowledgment of the Creator by every disbeliever is his submission, though unwilling (kurhan).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 84–86:

﴿Say, "We believe"﴾ The Prophet ﷺ was commanded to report about himself and his community that they believe. ﴿and in what has been sent down to us﴾ Here it is transitive with "ʿalā" (upon) to match His saying, "Say" (qul), whereas in al-Baqarah it is with "ilā" (to) to match His saying, "Say" (qūlū). This is because "ʿalā" is a particle of elevation, which requires descent from a height, and its descent in this sense is specific to the Prophet ﷺ. "Ilā" is a particle of endpoint, and it reaches the whole community. ﴿And whoever seeks﴾ (the verse): a nullification of all religions other than Islam. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 87–91:

﴿and of all mankind﴾: a general term used in the sense of the particular, referring to the believers; or it may be taken in its general sense, with the curse being in the Hereafter. ﴿Abiding therein﴾: the pronoun refers to the curse. It was also said that it refers to the Fire, even though it has not been mentioned, because the meaning requires it. ﴿Then they increased in disbelief﴾: it was said that they are the Jews, who disbelieved in ʿIsa (Jesus) after believing in Musa (Moses), then increased in disbelief by disbelieving in Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said that they disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) after having been believers before his mission, then increased in disbelief through their enmity towards him and their slander against him. It was also said that they are those who apostatized. ﴿Their repentance will never be accepted﴾: it was said that this is an expression for their dying upon disbelief, meaning that they have no repentance that could be accepted; this applies to specific people whom Allah sealed for disbelief. It was also said that their repentance will never be accepted while they persist in disbelief, and this is general. ﴿So never will be accepted from any of them an amount of earth [full of gold]﴾: a definite declaration of punishment for everyone who dies upon disbelief. As for the conjunction "wa" in His words ﴿and even if he should offer it in ransom﴾, it was said that it is superfluous (ziyadah); and it was said that it is for coordination (ʿatf) with an omitted element, as if he said: "He will not accept from any of them even if he gave it in charity (and even if he ransomed himself with it)." It was also said that He first negated acceptance absolutely in all its forms, then specified the ransom for negation, like your saying: "I will not do such-and-such at all, even if you were to beg me."

﴿Never will you attain righteousness﴾ meaning: you will not be among the righteous (al-abrar), and you will not attain complete righteousness, ﴿until you spend from that which you love﴾ of your wealth. The verse ﴿All food﴾ and what follows is a report that all foods were lawful for the Children of Israel, ﴿except what Israel had forbidden﴾, namely their father Ya'qub (Jacob), ﴿for himself﴾, which was the flesh and milk of camels. Then various kinds of food were made unlawful for them, such as fats and others, as a punishment for their disobedience. This also refutes their claim that they follow the religion (millah) of Ibrahim (Abraham), peace be upon him, and that the things that are now forbidden were forbidden to Ibrahim. It also contains evidence for the permissibility and occurrence of naskh (abrogation, the lifting of a previous ruling by a later one), because God made those things unlawful for them after they had been lawful. This goes against the Jews, who claim that abrogation is impossible regarding these things. It also contains a miracle of the Prophet ﷺ, since he reported this without having learned it from anyone. The reason Israel forbade camel meat to himself was that he fell ill, so he vowed that if God healed him, he would forbid the food he loved most, out of gratitude to God and to draw closer to Him. From this it is derived that it is permissible for prophets to make things unlawful for themselves through their own ijtihad (independent legal reasoning). ﴿Bring the Torah﴾ is a challenge to the Jews and an establishment of proof against them. It is narrated that they did not dare to bring out the Torah. ﴿Whoever fabricates﴾ means: whoever claims, after this clarification, that fats and other things were forbidden to the Children of Israel before the Torah was revealed, he is the wrongdoer and the one who obstinately opposes the truth with falsehood. ﴿God has spoken the truth﴾ means the matter is as He described it, not as you lie about it. In this there is an allusion to their lying. ﴿So follow the religion of Ibrahim﴾ is an obligation upon them to submit, as it is established that the religion of Islam is the religion of Ibrahim, in which nothing that is forbidden to them was made unlawful.

ع﴿Inna awwala bayt﴾ — meaning: the first mosque built on earth. Abu Dharr asked the Prophet ﷺ which mosque was built first. He said: "The Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram), then the Masjid al-Aqsa (Bayt al-Maqdis)." 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (رضي الله عنه) said: the meaning is that it is the first house placed (for people) as a blessing and as guidance, though there were houses before it.

﴿Bi-Bakka﴾ — it is said: this is Makkah, and the "ba'" (ب) is substituted for the "mim" (م). It is also said: Makkah is the entire Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), while Bakka is the mosque and what surrounds it.

﴿Mubarakan﴾ — accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Its governing element, according to 'Ali's view, is "wudi'a" (وضع, was placed): "Mubarakan" is a state of the pronoun within it (the implicit pronoun in "wudi'a"). According to the first view, it is a state of the genitive pronoun (the pronoun in the prepositional phrase "bi-Bakka"), and its governing element is the governing element of the prepositional phrase, namely the sense of "istiqrar" (being fixed/situated).

**﴿Therein are clear signs﴾** The signs of the House are many. Among them is the Station stone, which is the Maqam of Ibrahim (Abraham). He stood upon it when he raised the foundations of the House, and whenever the building grew higher, the stone rose with him into the air until the construction was completed, and Ibrahim's foot sank into the stone as if it were sinking into mud, and that trace remains to this day. Among them is that birds do not fly over it; among them is the destruction of the People of the Elephant; the repelling of tyrants from it; the gushing forth of Zamzam for Hajar, the mother of Isma'il, when Jibril struck the ground with his heel; and 'Abd al-Muttalib's digging of it after it had been buried, and that its water is beneficial for whatever it is drunk for; and so on.

**﴿the Station of Ibrahim﴾** It is said that it is a substitution (badl) for "the signs" or an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan). It is permissible for one to substitute for a plural because the Station contains many signs, as it indicates the power of God the Exalted, the prophethood of Ibrahim, and other things. It is also said that the signs are: the Station of Ibrahim and the security of whoever enters it. According to this, His saying ﴿and whoever enters it﴾ is a conjunction ('atf), and according to the first view it is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf). It is also said that the estimated sense is: "among them is the Station of Ibrahim," so it is then a subject (mubtada'), and the Station is the stone mentioned. It is said that it is the whole House, and it is said that it is all of Makkah.

**﴿was secure﴾** That is, secure from punishment. In the Jahiliyyah, if someone committed a crime and then sought refuge in the House, he would not be pursued or punished. In Islam, however, the Sanctuary does not prevent the application of the prescribed penalties (hudud) or retaliation (qisas). Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Hanifa said: that ruling remains in Islam, except that whoever is liable to a prescribed penalty or retaliation and enters the Sanctuary is not to be fed or sold anything until he leaves. It is also said: secure from the Fire.

**﴿Pilgrimage to the House﴾** This is an explanation of the obligation of Hajj. Scholars differed over whether it is required immediately (al-fawr) or may be delayed (al-tarakhi). The verse also contains a refutation of the Jews, who claimed to follow the religion of Ibrahim. It was said to them: if you are truthful, then make pilgrimage to the House that Ibrahim built and to which he called the people.

**﴿for whoever is able﴾** It is a substitution (badl) from "the people." It is also said that it is the agent (fa'il) of the verbal noun (masdar), which is hajj. It is also said that it is a conditional subject (shart mubtada'), meaning: whoever is able, then upon him is the Hajj. According to Malik, ability (istita'ah) is the capacity to reach Makkah with bodily health, whether on foot or mounted, together with sufficient provision and a safe road. It is said that ability is provision and a riding animal, which is the view of al-Shafi'i and 'Abd al-Malik ibn Habib, and a weak hadith has been narrated concerning this.

**﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾** It is said that the meaning is: whoever does not perform Hajj; it is expressed as disbelief to emphasize its gravity, like the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever abandons prayer has disbelieved." It is also said that it refers to the Jews, because they do not perform Hajj. It is also said: whoever claims that Hajj is not obligatory.

**﴿Why do you disbelieve﴾** A rebuke to the Jews.

**﴿Why do you bar﴾** Also a rebuke. They used to prevent people from entering Islam and sought to tempt the Muslims away from their religion.

**﴿the way of Allah﴾** Here it means Islam.

**﴿seeking to make it crooked﴾** The pronoun refers to the way, meaning: you seek crookedness for it.

**﴿while you are witnesses﴾** [Al 'Imran: 70] That is, you bear witness that Islam is true.

Among them is that birds do not fly over it; among them is the destruction of the People of the Elephant; the repelling of tyrants from it; the gushing forth of Zamzam for Hajar, the mother of Isma'il, when Jibril struck the ground with his heel; and 'Abd al-Muttalib's digging of it after it had been buried, and that its water is beneficial for whatever it is drunk for; and so on.

**﴿the Station of Ibrahim﴾** It is said that it is a substitution (badl) for "the signs" or an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan). It is permissible for one to substitute for a plural because the Station contains many signs, as it indicates the power of God the Exalted, the prophethood of Ibrahim, and other things. It is also said that the signs are: the Station of Ibrahim and the security of whoever enters it. According to this, His saying ﴿and whoever enters it﴾ is a conjunction ('atf), and according to the first view it is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf). It is also said that the estimated sense is: "among them is the Station of Ibrahim," so it is then a subject (mubtada'), and the Station is the stone mentioned. It is said that it is the whole House, and it is said that it is all of Makkah.

**﴿was secure﴾** That is, secure from punishment. In the Jahiliyyah, if someone committed a crime and then sought refuge in the House, he would not be pursued or punished. In Islam, however, the Sanctuary does not prevent the application of the prescribed penalties (hudud) or retaliation (qisas). Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Hanifa said: that ruling remains in Islam, except that whoever is liable to a prescribed penalty or retaliation and enters the Sanctuary is not to be fed or sold anything until he leaves. It is also said: secure from the Fire.

**﴿Pilgrimage to the House﴾** This is an explanation of the obligation of Hajj. Scholars differed over whether it is required immediately (al-fawr) or may be delayed (al-tarakhi). The verse also contains a refutation of the Jews, who claimed to follow the religion of Ibrahim. It was said to them: if you are truthful, then make pilgrimage to the House that Ibrahim built and to which he called the people.

**﴿for whoever is able﴾** It is a substitution (badl) from "the people." It is also said that it is the agent (fa'il) of the verbal noun (masdar), which is hajj. It is also said that it is a conditional subject (shart mubtada'), meaning: whoever is able, then upon him is the Hajj. According to Malik, ability (istita'ah) is the capacity to reach Makkah with bodily health, whether on foot or mounted, together with sufficient provision and a safe road. It is said that ability is provision and a riding animal, which is the view of al-Shafi'i and 'Abd al-Malik ibn Habib, and a weak hadith has been narrated concerning this.

**﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾** It is said that the meaning is: whoever does not perform Hajj; it is expressed as disbelief to emphasize its gravity, like the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever abandons prayer has disbelieved." It is also said that it refers to the Jews, because they do not perform Hajj. It is also said: whoever claims that Hajj is not obligatory.

**﴿Why do you disbelieve﴾** A rebuke to the Jews.

**﴿Why do you bar﴾** Also a rebuke. They used to prevent people from entering Islam and sought to tempt the Muslims away from their religion.

**﴿the way of Allah﴾** Here it means Islam.

**﴿seeking to make it crooked﴾** The pronoun refers to the way, meaning: you seek crookedness for it.

**﴿while you are witnesses﴾** [Al 'Imran: 70] That is, you bear witness that Islam is true.

﴿If you obey a party of those who were given the Scripture﴾, the verse: its wording is general, but the address is to the Aws and the Khazraj, since the Jews wanted to lead them astray. ﴿And how could you disbelieve?﴾ is a rebuke and an expression of astonishment. ﴿As He deserves to be feared﴾. It was said: it is abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a earlier ruling by a later one) by ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16]. It was also said: there is no abrogation, since there is no contradiction. Rather, the servants were commanded to be mindful of God in full measure within what they are able to do, as a safeguard against coercion and the like.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verse 103:**

﴿And hold fast to the rope of Allah﴾: i.e., hold firmly (tamassaku). The "rope" (al-habl) here is used metaphorically for the hand-grip one holds onto, and what is meant by it here is the Qur'an. It was also said that it means the community (al-jama'ah). ﴿And do not be divided﴾: this is a prohibition against mutual aversion and severing of ties, since the Aws had resolved to fight the Khazraj when the Jews sought to sow discord between them. It is possible that it is a prohibition against division in the fundamentals of religion (usul al-din), and that disagreement in the subsidiary matters (furu') does not fall under the prohibition. ﴿When you were enemies﴾: there was between the Aws and the Khazraj enmity and great wars, until Allah united them through Islam. ﴿And you were on the brink of a pit﴾: i.e., on the edge (harf) of a pit, and this is a simile for their state of disbelief and enmity, which would have led them to the Fire.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verse 104:

﴿Let there be among you a community﴾ etc.: This is evidence that enjoining good and forbidding evil is obligatory. His saying "among you" is evidence that it is a communal obligation (fard kifaya), because "min" (from) here indicates partiality. It has been said that it is for explaining the category, and that the meaning is: "Be a community." Changing evil is done by the hand, by the tongue, and by the heart, according to the circumstances.

﴿Like those who became divided﴾: they are the Jews and the Christians. Allah forbade the Muslims from being like them. It is related in a hadith that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Jews split into seventy-one sects, and the Christians split into seventy-two sects, and my community will split into seventy-three sects, all of them in the Fire except one." It was asked: "And which one is that?" He said: "Those who are upon what I and my Companions are upon."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verse 106:

﴿On the Day when some faces turn white﴾: the governing element (*al-'āmil*, the word in the sentence that governs this phrase grammatically) is omitted. It is said that the governing element is "a great punishment." ﴿Did you disbelieve after your faith?﴾ That is, it will be said to them: "Did you disbelieve?" The address is to those who apostatized from Islam. It is said that it is addressed to the Khawārij (an early sect that rebelled against 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib). It is also said that it is addressed to the Jews, because they believed in the attributes of the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned in the Torah, and then disbelieved in him when he was sent.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 110–111:

﴿You were the best nation﴾ Kana (كان) here is the one that implies permanence, like His saying, "And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful." It is also said: "You were" in the knowledge of Allah. It is also said: "You were" in what you were described with in the earlier Scriptures. It is also said: kuntum means antum (you are), and the address is to all the believers. It is also said: it is addressed to the Companions specifically. ﴿They will not harm you except with some insult﴾, i.e., with speech only, and that is the least of harms. ﴿They will turn their backs to you﴾ is a report of the unseen which has come into existence as a confirmed truth. ﴿Then they will not be helped﴾ is a new statement, not conjoined to "they will turn their backs." The benefit of this is that their turning their backs is restricted to the time of fighting, while the lack of victory is absolute. The clause is conjoined to the conditional clause (of the condition and its response), and thumma (then) is for the ordering of states, because their not being helped in an absolute sense is more severe than their turning their backs at the time of fighting.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 112–115:

﴿Except by a rope from Allah﴾. **Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 3, verse 117:**

﴿The likeness of what they spend﴾, etc. This is a simile for the spending of the disbelievers, likened to a crop destroyed by a cold wind, so its owners gain nothing from it. Likewise, the disbelievers gain nothing from what they spend. The sentence contains an ellipsis (ḥadhf, omission of words understood from context), and its estimated form is: "The likeness of what they spend is like the likeness of a destroying wind," or "The likeness of the destruction of what they spend is like the likeness of the destruction by a wind." This was needed because what they spend is not being likened to the wind. Rather, it is likened to the crop that the wind destroyed. ﴿ṣirr﴾ means cold. ﴿The crop of a people who wronged themselves﴾ means they disobeyed God, so He punished them by destroying their crop. ﴿And God did not wrong them﴾: the pronoun refers either to the disbelievers, or to the hypocrites, or to the owners of the crop. The first is more preferred, because His saying ﴿أنفسهم يظلمون﴾ ("they wrong themselves") is a present-tense verb (fi'l ḥāl), which indicates that it refers to those present.

"Bitanatan min dunikum" (بِطَانَةً مِّن دُونِكُمْ): meaning, intimate confidants (awliya') from outside your own community. The sense is a prohibition against taking the disbelievers as intimate confidants and allies.

It is said that a man once told Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "There is a Christian here who has no equal in fine penmanship; would he not write for you?" He replied: "Then I would be taking as an intimate confidant someone other than the believers."

﴿They spare no effort to corrupt you﴾: that is, they do not fall short in causing you ruin. Khabal (الخبال) means corruption.

﴿They love what distresses you﴾: that is, they wish you harm. Ma (ما) here is a verbal-masdar particle (ma masdariyya), and this clause and the one before it are either a description of the intimate confidants or a fresh, independent statement.

﴿You believe in the Book, all of it﴾: that is, in every Book Allah has sent down, whereas the Jews do not believe in your Qur'an.

﴿They bite their fingertips at you in rage﴾: an expression for intense rage combined with inability to act on it. Al-anamil (الأنامل) is the plural of anamila (أنملة), which may be pronounced with a dammah or a fathah on the letter mim.

﴿Die in your rage!﴾: a rebuke and an expression of vexation. It is also said to be a supplication.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 120–121:

﴿If good befalls you, it grieves them; but if misfortune strikes you, they rejoice at it.﴾ Al-hasanah (good) here means the blessings, such as victory, provision and other things; and al-sayyi'ah (evil) is its opposite. ﴿It will not harm you at all﴾, from al-dayr, meaning al-darr (harm).

﴿And when you set out early in the morning from your family﴾: it was revealed concerning the Battle of Uhud. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to fight in the morning of Saturday, and he left Madinah on Friday after the prayer. He had consulted his companions before the prayer. ﴿You were assigning the believers to their positions﴾: that is, settling them, and this was on Saturday when the fighting was present. It was also said that this was on Friday after the prayer, when he went out from Madinah, but this is weak, because one does not say "ghadawta" (you set out early) for what comes after midday except figuratively. It was also said that this was on Friday before the prayer, when he consulted the people, but this is weak, because he did not then assign positions for fighting, unless it is meant that he settled them by arrangement at the time of the consultation. ﴿Positions﴾: places, and it is the plural of maq'ad (position/seat).

**Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah Al ʿImran, verses 122–124:**

﴿Two groups among you﴾: they were Banu Harithah from the Aws and Banu Salamah from the Khazraj. When they saw the large number of the polytheists and the small number of the believers, they resolved to withdraw. But Allah protected them, and they went forth with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿Lose heart﴾: *al-fashl* (loss of resolve) is fatigue in the body, and in judgment it is incapacity, bewilderment, and corruption of resolve. ﴿And Allah is their Protector﴾: that is, their Supporter who keeps them firm. Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah said: "We would not have wished that this verse had not been revealed, because of the words ﴿And Allah is their Protector.﴾"

﴿And Allah had already helped you at Badr﴾: a reminder of Allah's help to them on the day of Badr, so that their hearts would be strengthened. ﴿While you were weak﴾: *al-dhillah* (weakness) is the smallness of their number and the frailty of their equipment. On the day of Badr they were three hundred and thirteen men, and they had only one horse, while the polytheists were between nine hundred and a thousand, and they had one hundred horses. Seventy of the polytheists were killed, seventy were taken captive, and the rest of them were routed.

﴿So that you may be grateful﴾: this is connected either to "He helped you" or to "fear Allah." The first is more apparent.

﴿When you said to the believers﴾: this statement was made on the day of Badr, and it was said that it was on the day of Uhud. The governing element of *idh* (when) is, on the first view, omitted; on the second view, it is a substitute for *idh ghadawta* (when you set out in the morning).

﴿Is it not sufficient for you﴾: this is an affirmation whose answer is "Yes." The speaker's reply is given in this form to confirm the matter and make it clear, as in His saying: Say, ﴿Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth? Say: Allah﴾ [al-Raʿd: 16].
