**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 3, verses 125–128**

﴿And they come upon you immediately﴾. The pronoun refers to the polytheists. *al-Fawr* means haste: that is, "from that very moment." It was also said that the meaning is "from their journey."

﴿with five thousand angels﴾: more than the number that would suffice you, so that this would increase your strength. If this refers to the Day of Badr, then the angels did fight on that day. If it refers to the Day of Uhud, then the condition was stated in His words: ﴿if you are patient and mindful of God﴾. When they broke the condition, the angels were not sent down.

﴿marked﴾, with the *waw* pronounced with a fatha or with a kasra (*musawwimin* or *musawwamin*), meaning "distinguished," or "marking themselves" or "marking their horses." The distinguishing mark of the angels on the Day of Badr was white turbans, except Jibril, whose turban was yellow. It was also said that their turbans were yellow, and that their horses had docked tails. It was also said that they rode piebald horses (*bulq*).

﴿And God did not make it﴾: the pronoun refers to the sending down or to the reinforcement.

﴿and so that your hearts might be at rest﴾ is coordinated with *bushra* ("good news"), because this verb is in the sense of a verbal noun. It was also said that it is governed by a hidden verb indicated by *ja'alahu* ("made it").

﴿so that He might cut off﴾ is governed either by His words ﴿And God had already helped you﴾ or by His words ﴿And victory is not from anything but God﴾.

﴿You have no share in the affair at all﴾ is a parenthetical sentence placed between the two coordinated elements. It was revealed when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) invoked curses, during the prayer, against some tribes of the Arabs, and then gave up cursing them.

﴿or He will turn to them [in forgiveness]﴾: its meaning is that they will become Muslims.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 3, verses 125–128**

﴿And they come upon you immediately﴾. The pronoun refers to the polytheists. *al-Fawr* means haste: that is, "from that very moment." It was also said that the meaning is "from their journey."

﴿so that He might cut off﴾ is governed either by His words ﴿And God had already helped you﴾ or by His words ﴿And victory is not from anything but God﴾.

﴿You have no share in the affair at all﴾ is a parenthetical sentence placed between the two coordinated elements. It was revealed when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) invoked curses, during the prayer, against some tribes of the Arabs, and then gave up cursing them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 130–133:

﴿Multiplied manifold﴾ They used to increase what was due year after year. ﴿Hasten﴾ (read) without a conjunction, as a fresh statement; and with the conjunction "wa" (and), as a coordination with what preceded. ﴿To forgiveness﴾, that is, to the deeds by which you deserve forgiveness. ﴿Its breadth﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: the heavens and the earth are joined to one another, as garments are joined together, and that is the breadth of Paradise, while none knows its length except Allah. It was also said: "breadth" here is not the opposite of "length"; rather the meaning is its vastness, like the vastness of the heavens and the earth.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 139–141:

﴿وَلاَ تَهِنُوا﴾ (Do not be feeble) is a strengthening of the hearts of the believers. ﴿وَأَنْتُمُ الأَعْلَوْنَ﴾ (and you will have the upper hand) is a report of the supremacy of the word of Islam. ﴿إِن يَمْسَسْكُمْ قَرْحٌ﴾ (If a wound touches you) and the verse means: if you were struck by killing or wounds at Uhud, then the disbelievers were touched by the like of it at Badr. It is also said: the disbelievers were touched on the day of Uhud by the like of what touched you in it, for they inflicted harm upon you and you inflicted harm upon them, and this is a consolation to the believers through sharing in the same affliction. ﴿نُدَاوِلُهَا﴾ (We alternate them) is also a consolation regarding what happened on the day of Uhud. ﴿وَلِيَعْلَمَ﴾ (and that Allah may know) is connected to an omitted element, its meaning being: what afflicted you was what afflicted them on the day of Uhud, so that Allah may know; and the meaning is that He may know that manifestly, as a knowledge by which the proof is established for you. ﴿شُهَدَآءَ﴾ (martyrs) refers to those among the Muslims who were killed on the day of Uhud. ﴿وَلِيُمَحِّصَ ٱللَّهُ﴾ (and that Allah may purify) means: He may make clear; it is also said: He may distinguish. It is coordinated with the previously mentioned reasons for the story of Uhud, and the meaning is that the disbelievers' gaining the upper hand over the Muslims is only for the purification of the believers, and that the victory of the believers over the disbelievers is only so that Allah may destroy the disbelievers, that is, annihilate them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verse 142–143:

﴿Or did you think﴾ "Am" here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), taken as implying "bal" (rather) and the hamzah, according to Sibawayh. This verse and what follows is a rebuke to some of the believers, from whom certain things proceeded on the day of Uhud. ﴿You wished for death﴾ This was addressed to a group who had missed the battle of Badr, so they wished to be present at fighting the disbelievers with the Prophet (ﷺ), in order to make up for what they had missed of jihad. Accordingly, what they wished for was jihad, which is the cause of death. It was also said: what they wished for was martyrdom in the way of Allah.

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 3, verse 144:

﴿Muhammad is only a messenger﴾. The meaning is that Muhammad ﷺ is a messenger like the other messengers; he has conveyed the message just as they conveyed theirs, so it is obligatory upon you to hold fast to his religion both during his life and after his death. The occasion of this was that a crier cried out on the day of Uhud: "Muhammad has been killed," and some of the people were shaken. ﴿Will you then turn back on your heels if he dies?﴾ The alif of reproach (alif al-tawbikh) entered upon the conditional clause, and the fa' (fa') entered to link the conditional sentence with the sentence preceding it. The meaning is that the death of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, or his being killed, does not necessitate that his companions turn back on their heels, because his law has been established and his proofs have been confirmed. So He rebuked them on the supposition that a turning back might proceed from them should he die ﷺ or be killed, though it was known that he would not be killed; but He mentioned this because of what the crier had cried out and what had taken hold of their souls. ﴿The grateful ones﴾. Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Those who remain steadfast upon their religion."

﴿كِتَٰباً مُّؤَجَّلاً﴾ [a decree with a fixed term]: it is in the accusative (naṣb) as a maṣdar (verbal noun, cognate accusative), because the meaning is: "He decreed death as a decree (kataba al-mawt kitāban)." Ibn 'Aṭiyya said that it is in the accusative as a tamyīz (specification, an accusative that clarifies the noun it follows). ﴿نُؤْتِهِ مِنْهَا﴾ [We will give him of it]: that is, of the reward of this world. It is restricted by the will of Allah, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿We hasten for him therein what We will, for whomever We intend﴾ [al-Isrā': 18].

The verb is attributed to the pronoun of the Prophet, and "with him are rabbis (rabbiyyun)" is then in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). It has also been said that the verb is attributed to the rabbiyyun, so that "rabbiyyun" would be the object of the passive verb (ma lam yusamma fa'iluh, the form whose doer is not named). On the first view, one stops at the word "qatala" (fought/was killed). The first view is preferred because of what the crier cried out on the day of Uhud: "Muhammad has indeed been killed." So the example is given of a prophet who was killed. The second view is preferred because no prophet was ever killed in battle.

﴿Rabbiyyun﴾ means scholars, like "rabbaniyyun" (godly scholars). It has also been said that it means large groups.

﴿Fa-ma wahanu﴾: the pronoun refers to the rabbiyyun, on the basis that the killing is attributed to the Prophet. On the basis that the killing is attributed to them, the pronoun refers to those of them who were not killed.

﴿Wa-ma istakanu﴾ means they did not submit in humiliation to the disbelievers. Some grammarians (nuhat, the early Arabic grammarians) said: "istikan" is derived from "sukun" (stillness), and its pattern is "if'alu", with the vowel on the kaf lengthened, so that from lengthening it a long alif came into being, as in the case of "ishbaʿ" (full vowelling). It has also been said that it derives from "kana yakunu" (to be), so its pattern is "istaf'alu".

The statement of Allah, ﴿fa-ma wahanu﴾ and what follows it, is a reproach directed at what some people did on the day of Uhud.

﴿Wa-thabbit aqdamana﴾ means: in the battle.

﴿Thawab al-dunya﴾ means victory.

﴿Thawab al-akhirah﴾ means Paradise.

﴿In tuti'u alladhina kafaru﴾: they are the hypocrites who said what they said regarding the matter of Uhud. It has also been said that they are the polytheists of Quraysh, and it has been said that they are the Jews.

﴿ٱلرُّعْبَ﴾ It was said: Allah cast terror into the hearts of the polytheists at Uhud, so they returned to Makkah without any cause. It was also said: when they were part of the way, they intended to turn back in order to annihilate the Muslims, but Allah cast terror into their hearts, so they held back. The verse encompasses all the disbelievers, based on the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I have been granted victory through terror."

﴿وَلَقَدْ صَدَقَكُمُ ٱللَّهُ وَعْدَهُ﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had promised the Muslims victory from Allah. Allah granted them victory at first, the polytheists were routed, and twenty-two men of them were killed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had commanded the archers to hold their positions and not leave them. When they saw the polytheists had been routed, they coveted the spoils and pursued them, and they opposed what they had been commanded regarding remaining in their place. So the defeat turned against the Muslims. ﴿إِذْ تَحُسُّونَهُمْ﴾ means: you were killing them with a devastating slaughter, namely at the beginning of the affair. ﴿وَتَنَٰزَعْتُمْ﴾ A dispute occurred among the archers, so some of them remained steadfast as they had been commanded, and some of them did not remain steadfast. ﴿وَعَصَيْتُمْ﴾ means: you opposed what you had been commanded regarding remaining steadfast. This address came to all the believers, although only some of them opposed, as an admonition to all and a concealment for those who did that. The answer of إذ (idh) is omitted, and its estimated meaning is: you would have been defeated. ﴿مِنكُم مَّن يُرِيدُ الدُّنْيَا﴾ these are the ones who were eager for the spoils with him. ﴿لِيَبْتَلِيَكُمْ﴾ means: so that what happened to you of killing and purification (tamhis, meaning sifting or refining) would befall you. ﴿وَلَقَدْ عَفَا عَنْكُمْ﴾ is an announcement that the sin deserved more than what befell them, had it not been for Allah's pardon of them. Its meaning is: He indeed spared you. It was also said: it is a pardon for the sin.

﴿When you were climbing up﴾. The verb governing *idh* (إذ) is *ʿafā* (عفا, "He pardoned"), so *idh tuṣʿidūna* is connected to what precedes it. It is also possible that the governing verb is an implied one (*muḍmar*).

﴿And not turning back for anyone﴾ is an intensification describing the state of flight.

﴿While the Messenger was calling you﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: "Come to me, servants of Allah!" but they were fleeing.

﴿From behind you﴾ means from behind you. This contains praise for the Prophet (ﷺ), for *al-ukhrā* (الأخرى, "the rear") is the position of the brave.

﴿So He rewarded you﴾, that is, He recompensed you, ﴿with grief upon grief﴾. It has been said: He rewarded you with grief because of the grief you caused the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, when you disobeyed and disputed. It has also been said: He rewarded you with grief that followed grief. One of the two griefs was what befell them of killing and wounds, and the other was what was rumoured about the killing of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿Over what had escaped you﴾ of victory and spoils of war, ﴿nor over what had befallen you﴾ of killing, wounds, and defeat.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 154–155:

﴿Security, a slumber that overtook them﴾. Ibn Mas'ud said: "We dozed off on the day of Uhud, and slumber during battle is a security from Allah." ﴿It overtook a group of you﴾: they were the sincere believers; slumber overcame them as reassurance for them. ﴿And another group, whom their own selves had worried﴾: they were the hypocrites, who were afraid that Abu Sufyan and the polytheists would return to them. ﴿Thinking about Allah other than the truth﴾: its meaning is that they thought Islam was not true and that Allah would not give them victory. ﴿The thought of ignorance﴾ is an apposition (badal), and it is by omission of the qualified noun; its estimated form is "the thought of ignorant affection" or "the thought of ignorant division." ﴿Do we have any say in the matter at all?﴾ This was said by Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, and the meaning is: we have no opinion, and our word is not heard; or: we have nothing of the true matter, so their saying on this reading would be disbelief. ﴿They conceal within themselves what they do not reveal to you﴾: this may refer to the statements they made or to disbelief. ﴿If we had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here﴾: this was said by Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, and it may carry the same meaning as the statement of Abdullah ibn Ubayy. ﴿Say: Even if you had been in your houses﴾, the verse: a rebuttal to them and an announcement that the term of every person is one fixed term, that whoever is not killed dies at his appointed time and it is not postponed, and that whoever is destined to be killed, nothing will save him from it. ﴿And that Allah might test﴾ is connected to a verb estimated as: "He did that to you so that He might test." ﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away﴾, the verse: it was revealed concerning those who fled on the day of Uhud. ﴿Caused them to slip﴾, that is, sought to make them slip; it may also mean: "made them slip," i.e., caused them to fall into error. ﴿Because of some of what they had earned﴾, that is, they had sins for which Allah punished them, by empowering Satan to make them slip. ﴿Allah has pardoned them﴾, that is, He forgave them for what they had fallen into of fleeing.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 156–158:

﴿Do not be like those who disbelieved﴾, i.e., the hypocrites (al-munafiqun), ﴿concerning their brothers﴾: this is the brotherhood of kinship, because the hypocrites were from the Aws and the Khazraj, and most of those killed on the day of Uhud were from them; only four of the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun) were killed. ﴿When they travel through the land﴾, i.e., they journeyed. He said "idha" (when), which denotes the future, with "qalu" (they said), because it is in the narration of a past situation. ﴿Or were raiders﴾: the plural of ghazi (raider), whose form is fu"‘‘al (fu''‘‘al), with a damma on the fa' and a shadda on the ‘ayn. ﴿Had they remained with us﴾: this is a corrupt belief on their part, because they thought that their brothers, had they been with them, would not have died and would not have been killed. This is the view of one who does not believe in predestination (al-qadar) and the fixed term (al-ajal al-mahtum), and it is close to the doctrine of the Mu'tazila in their saying that there are two terms (al-ajalayn). ﴿That He may make it﴾: this is connected to "qalu" (they said). That is, they said that, so it became a grief in their hearts; the lam is the lam of outcome (lam al-sayrura), to explain the consequence. ﴿That﴾: a reference to their saying and their corrupt belief, which caused them grief, because the one who is certain of predestination and the fixed term has grief removed from him. ﴿And Allah gives life and causes death﴾: a refutation of their saying and their belief. ﴿And if you are killed﴾ (the verse): a statement that the forgiveness of Allah and His mercy for them, if they are killed and die in the way of Allah, is better for them than what they accumulate of the worldly life. ﴿And if you die or are killed﴾ (the verse): a statement that whoever dies or is killed, he will be gathered to Allah.

﴿فَبِمَا رَحْمَةٍ﴾ *(So it was by mercy)* "ما" (ma) here is an extra particle (ma za'ida) for emphasis.
﴿لاَنْفَضُّواْ﴾ *(they would have dispersed)*, meaning they would have scattered.
﴿فَٱعْفُ عَنْهُمْ﴾ *(so pardon them)* in matters that concern you personally.
﴿وَٱسْتَغْفِرْ لَهُمْ﴾ *(and ask forgiveness for them)* in matters that concern the right of Allah.
﴿وَشَاوِرْهُمْ﴾ *(and consult them)*. Consultation (mushawara) is legally commanded. The Prophet (ﷺ) consulted people for their opinion in wars and other matters, but not in the legal rulings of the Sharia. Ibn 'Abbas said: "And consult them in some of the affair."
﴿فَإِذَا عَزَمْتَ فَتَوَكَّلْ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ﴾ *(And when you have made a decision, then rely upon Allah)*. Tawakkul (reliance, trust in Allah) is depending on Allah to obtain benefits or to preserve them after they are obtained, and to repel harms or remove them after they have occurred. It is among the highest stations, for two reasons. The first is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who rely upon Him﴾. The second is the guarantee in His saying: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him﴾ [al-Talaq: 3]. It may be obligatory, according to His saying: ﴿And upon Allah rely, if you are believers﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 23], where He made it a condition of faith. The apparent meaning is His saying, exalted is His majesty: ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾ [Al 'Imran: 122], since the command is taken to indicate obligation.

Know that people in tawakkul are of three levels. The first: that the servant relies upon his Lord as a person relies upon his trusted agent, whose sincere advice he does not doubt and who manages his affairs. The second: that the servant is with his Lord as a child is with its mother, for it knows no one else and resorts to no one but her. The third: that the servant is with his Lord as a corpse is before the washer, having entirely surrendered himself to Him. The person of the first level still has a share of looking to his own self, unlike the person of the second level. The person of the second level still has a share of desire and choice, unlike the person of the third level. These levels are built upon the special Tawhid (tawhid al-khass) that we discussed in His saying: ﴿And your God is one God﴾ [al-Baqara: 163]. They grow strong with its strength and weaken with its weakness.

If it is said: Is abandoning the means (asbab) a condition of tawakkul or not? The answer is that the means are of three kinds. The first is a means known with certainty, which Allah has established. Abandoning it is not permitted, such as eating to repel hunger and wearing clothing to repel cold. The second is a presumed means, such as trade and seeking livelihood and the like. Doing it does not precede tawakkul, because tawakkul is an act of the heart, not of the body, and it is permissible to abandon it for one who is strong enough to do so. The third is a distant, doubtful means, and doing it precedes tawakkul.

Beyond tawakkul is tafwid (complete entrusting), which is full submission to the command of Allah, exalted is He. The one who relies has a desire and a choice, and he seeks his desire by depending on his Lord. As for the one who entrusts, he has no desire and no choice; rather, he attributes desire and choice to Allah, exalted is He. So he is more perfect in adab with Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 3, verses 161–163:

﴿It is not for a prophet to misappropriate (yaghull)﴾. It derives from *ghulul*, which is taking something secretly from the spoils of war or from other property. It has also been read with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a *damma* on the *ghayn* (*yaghull*), and its meaning is to absolve the Prophet ﷺ of *ghulul*. The reason for the revelation is that a red woollen cloak (*qatifa hamra'*) was lost from the spoils, and some hypocrites said, "Perhaps the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took it." Nafi' and others read it with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *fatha* on the *ghayn* (*yughalla*), meaning: it is not permitted for anyone to misappropriate a prophet, i.e., to betray him regarding the spoils. The Prophet is singled out for mention, although this prohibition applies in general, because the offence is more grave when committed against the Prophet, since sins are magnified in his presence. It was also said that the meaning of this reading is: that one finds him to be a misappropriator, just as you say *ahmadtu al-rajul* when you find the man to be praiseworthy (*mahmud*). According to this view, the meaning of this reading returns to the meaning of the reading with a *fatha* on the *ya'*.

﴿And whoever misappropriates will come with what he misappropriated﴾: a threat to whoever misappropriates, that on the Day of Resurrection he will be driven carrying on his neck the thing he misappropriated. This has been explained in a hadith, where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Let me not find any of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with a camel on his neck, let me not find any of you with a horse on his neck, let me not find any of you with sheets (*ruqa'*) on his neck, let me not find any of you with gold or silver (*samit*) on his neck, let me not find any of you with a person on his neck who says, 'O Messenger of Allah, help me!' and I say, 'I possess nothing for you against Allah; I have conveyed (the message) to you.'"

﴿Then is one who followed﴾ — the verse: it has been said that the one who followed the pleasure of Allah is the one who did not misappropriate, and the one who incurred the wrath is the one who misappropriated. It was also said that the one who followed the pleasure is the one who was martyred at Uhud, and the one who incurred the wrath is the hypocrites who turned back from the expedition. ﴿They are of degrees (darajat)﴾: possessors of degrees. The meaning is the difference between the ranks of the people of pleasure and the people of wrath, or the difference among the degrees of the people of pleasure, since some of them are above others; likewise the degrees of the people of wrath.

This has been explained in a hadith, where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Let me not find any of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with a camel on his neck, let me not find any of you with a horse on his neck, let me not find any of you with sheets (*ruqa'*) on his neck, let me not find any of you with gold or silver (*samit*) on his neck, let me not find any of you with a person on his neck who says, 'O Messenger of Allah, help me!' and I say, 'I possess nothing for you against Allah; I have conveyed (the message) to you.'"

﴿Then is one who followed﴾ — the verse: it has been said that the one who followed the pleasure of Allah is the one who did not misappropriate, and the one who incurred the wrath is the one who misappropriated. It was also said that the one who followed the pleasure is the one who was martyred at Uhud, and the one who incurred the wrath is the hypocrites who turned back from the expedition. ﴿They are of degrees (darajat)﴾: possessors of degrees. The meaning is the difference between the ranks of the people of pleasure and the people of wrath, or the difference among the degrees of the people of pleasure, since some of them are above others; likewise the degrees of the people of wrath.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 3, verses 161–163:

﴿It is not for a prophet to misappropriate (yaghull)﴾. It derives from *ghulul*, which is taking something secretly from the spoils of war or from other property. It has also been read with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a *damma* on the *ghayn* (*yaghull*), and its meaning is to absolve the Prophet ﷺ of *ghulul*. The reason for the revelation is that a red woollen cloak (*qatifa hamra'*) was lost from the spoils, and some hypocrites said, "Perhaps the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took it." Nafi' and others read it with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *fatha* on the *ghayn* (*yughalla*), meaning: it is not permitted for anyone to misappropriate a prophet, i.e., to betray him regarding the spoils. The Prophet is singled out for mention, although this prohibition applies in general, because the offence is more grave when committed against the Prophet, since sins are magnified in his presence. It was also said that the meaning of this reading is: that one finds him to be a misappropriator, just as you say *ahmadtu al-rajul* when you find the man to be praiseworthy (*mahmud*). According to this view, the meaning of this reading returns to the meaning of the reading with a *fatha* on the *ya'*.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verse 164:

﴿Indeed, Allah conferred a favor upon the believers﴾ — the verse is a report of Allah's favor upon the believers in sending the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿from among themselves﴾. Its meaning is in lineage and language. That he is of their own kind (jins) necessitates familiarity with him and little aversion from him; that he speaks their language necessitates good understanding of what he conveys. And because he is one of them, they know his noble descent (hasab), his truthfulness, and his trustworthiness (ﷺ), and he (ﷺ) is more compassionate and merciful toward them than outsiders would be.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verse 165:

﴿Why, when a calamity struck you, though you had inflicted twice as much (on the enemy)﴾ — this is the verse. It is a rebuke to the Muslims for their words concerning those among them who were struck on the day of Uhud. The interrogative alif (alif al-tawbikh, the particle of reproach) has entered upon the conjunctive waw, and the sentence is conjoined to what preceded of the story of Uhud and to an omitted clause, ﴿though you had inflicted twice as much (on the enemy)﴾. On the day of Uhud, seventy of the Muslims were killed, and seventy of the polytheists had been killed on the day of Badr, and seventy had been taken captive. ﴿It is from yourselves﴾. It has been said: its meaning is that they were punished with defeat for opposing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he wished to remain in Madinah and not go out to the polytheists, but they refused except to go out. And it has been said: rather, that refers to the disobedience of the archers, as has been mentioned earlier.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 166–167:

﴿On the day when the two hosts met﴾, i.e., the host of the Muslims and the host of the polytheists on the day of Uhud. ﴿And it was said to them: "Come, fight in the way of Allah, or repel [the enemy]"﴾ [3:167]: The opinion of Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul was that the Muslims should not go out against the polytheists. When a group of the Muslims asked to go out, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out, and Abdullah became angry and said: "He obeyed them and disobeyed us." So he turned back, and three hundred and fifty men turned back with him. Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Haram al-Ansari followed in their footsteps and said to them: "Come back, fight in the way of Allah, or repel [the enemy]." Abdullah ibn Ubayy said to him: "I do not think there would be fighting. Had we known that there would be fighting, we would have been with you."

﴿Or repel [the enemy]﴾, i.e., increase the numbers, even if you do not fight.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 168–171:

﴿Those who said﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "those who were hypocrites," or [it refers to] "their brothers" by lineage, because they were from the Aws and the Khazraj. ﴿Say: "Then avert"﴾ means: repel [death]; the meaning is a reply to them. ﴿Rather, they are alive﴾ is an announcement that the state of the martyrs is the state of the living, in enjoying the provisions of Paradise. This is unlike the rest of the believing dead, for they enjoy provisions only until they enter Paradise on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them﴾: the meaning is that they rejoice in their brothers who remained in the world after them, because they hope that they too will be martyred and thus attain the same martyrdom that they attained. ﴿That there is no fear﴾ is in the position of the object (maf'ul) or a substitute for "those who" [in] ﴿they rejoice﴾; it is repeated to mention the blessing and bounty connected to it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 172–173:

﴿Those who responded to God and the Messenger﴾ is either a description of the believers or a subject whose predicate is ﴿for those who did good among them and feared God, there is a great reward﴾, and the verse goes on. It was revealed concerning those who went out with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in pursuit of the polytheists after the battle of Uhud. He went with them as far as Hamra' al-Asad, which is eight miles from Madina, and he stayed there three days. They had been struck by wounds and hardships, yet they steeled themselves and went out, so God praised them for that. ﴿Those to whom people said﴾ and the verse goes on: when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out to Hamra' al-Asad after Uhud, this reached Abu Sufyan. A caravan of 'Abd al-Qays, heading for Madina to trade for provisions, passed by him, so he offered them a camel-load of raisins on condition that they discourage the Muslims from pursuing the polytheists. They frightened them with the polytheists, but they said: ﴿God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾ and they went out. So the first "people" are the caravan of 'Abd al-Qays, and the second "people" are the polytheists of Quraysh. It is also said that Abu Sufyan called out on the day of Uhud: "Our appointment is at Badr next year." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If God wills." When the following year came, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out to Badr for the appointment, and Abu Sufyan sent Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i to discourage the Muslims. On this view, the first "people" is Nu'aym. He was called "people" though he was one man, because he was of the kind of people, as you would say, "I rode the horses" when you rode a single steed. ﴿So it increased them﴾: the subject is a pronoun referring to the object, namely "the people have gathered against you, so fear them." The correct view is that faith increases and decreases, so its meaning here is the strengthening of their certainty and their trust in God. ﴿God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾: a phrase by which one repels what one fears and dislikes. It is the phrase Abraham (peace be upon him) said when he was thrown into the fire. The meaning of ﴿God is sufficient for us﴾ is: He alone suffices us, so we fear no other. The meaning of ﴿and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾ is praise of God, and that He is the best one in whom a servant places his trust and to whom he turns for refuge.

﴿فَٱنْقَلَبُواْ﴾ [*So they returned*], that is, they returned with the blessing of safety and the bounty of reward. ﴿وَٱتَّبَعُواْ رِضْوَٰنَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ [*and followed the pleasure of Allah*] by going out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿ذٰلِكُمُ ٱلشَّيْطَٰنُ﴾ [*That is the Satan*]: here it refers to Abu Sufyan, or to Nu'aym whom Abu Sufyan sent, or to Iblis. ﴿ذٰلِكُمُ﴾ [*that*] is a *mubtada'* (subject of the nominal sentence), and ﴿ٱلشَّيْطَٰنُ﴾ [*the Satan*] is its *khabar* (predicate), and what follows is a new (*mustanaf*) sentence. Alternatively, ﴿ٱلشَّيْطَٰنُ﴾ is a *na't* (descriptive adjunct) and what follows is the *khabar*.

﴿يُخَوِّفُ أَوْلِيَاءَهُ﴾ [*he frightens his allies*]: that is, he frightens you, O believers, of his allies, who are the disbelievers. The first object (*maf'ul awwal*) is therefore omitted, and it is indicated by His saying ﴿فَلاَ تَخَافُوهُمْ﴾ [*so do not fear them*]. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas read it as ﴿يخوفكم أولياءه﴾ (*yukhawwifukum awliyā'ahu*), [*he frightens you of his allies*]. It has also been said that the meaning is: he frightens the hypocrites, who are his allies, from the disbelievers of Quraysh. On this reading, the second object (*maf'ul thani*) is omitted.

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 176–178:

﴿And do not let them grieve you﴾: a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ). It is also read with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the zay wherever it occurs as a present-tense verb, from the second form of ḥazana (yaḥzunu), and this is more common in the language than aḥzana. ﴿Those who race to disbelief﴾: that is, they hasten toward its sayings and deeds, and they are the hypocrites and the disbelievers. ﴿Indeed, those who have purchased﴾ (the verse): they are those mentioned before, or it is general over all disbelievers. ﴿That what We grant them respite is better for them﴾: that is, We give them time. That (anna) is the object of yaḥsabanna, and mā is the ism of anna, so its proper form is to be written separately, and khayr is its predicate. ﴿That what We grant them respite﴾: here mā is kāffa (it prevents anna from governing), and the meaning is a refutation of them: the granting of respite to them is not good for them; it is only a gradual leading-on (istidrāj) so that they may accumulate sin.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verse 179:

﴿It is not for Allah to leave the believers in the state you are in﴾ — the verse is addressed to the believers. The meaning: Allah would not leave the believers mixed together with the hypocrites (munafiqun), but He distinguished these from those by what appeared at the Battle of Uhud of statements and actions that indicate either faith or hypocrisy. ﴿Nor is it for Allah to inform you of the unseen﴾ — that is, Allah would not inform you of what is in the hearts of faith or hypocrisy, or that you would be victorious or defeated. ﴿But Allah chooses from His messengers whom He wills﴾ — that is, He chooses from among His messengers whomever He wills and informs them of whatever He wills of His unseen.

﴿Those who withhold﴾ — they refuse to pay zakat and other [obligations]. ﴿it is better for them﴾ — "it" (huwa) is a separator (fasl) meaning "it is the excess/bounty," and khayran is the second object (maf'ul thani); the first object is omitted, its implied sense being: "Let not the withholding (al-bukhl) be thought (la yahsabanna al-bukhla) to be good for them."

﴿they will be encircled﴾ — i.e., they will be bound to the sin of what they withheld. It has also been said: what they withheld will be made into a serpent which will be coiled around their necks on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verse 181:

﴿Indeed, Allah has heard﴾ the statement: When the verse ﴿Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245] was revealed, some of the Jews, namely Finhas, or Huyayy ibn Akhtab, or others, said: "Only the poor borrow from the rich. Allah is poor and we are rich." So this verse was revealed. That statement was an objection to the Qur'an, caused by their lack of understanding or their distortion of meanings. If they said it out of genuine belief, it is disbelief [added to their disbelief]; and if they said it without belief, it is contempt and obstinacy. ﴿We will record what they have said﴾, meaning the angels will write it down in the scrolls. ﴿And their killing of the prophets﴾, meaning the killing of the prophets by their forefathers. It is attributed to them because they are content with it and follow those of their forefathers who did it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 183–184:

﴿Those who say﴾ is an attributive clause describing "those who", and not an attributive clause describing "the servants". ﴿"Until He brings us an offering (qurban) which the fire consumes."﴾ When they wished to know whether God accepted their charity or anything else, they would place it in a certain spot, and fire would descend from the sky and burn it. If it did not descend, the offering was not accepted. They claimed that God had made this a sign of the truthfulness of the messengers. ﴿Say: "Messengers have already come to you before me with clear proofs and even with what you speak of, so why did you kill them, if you are truthful?"﴾ This is a refutation of them: the messengers came to them with miracles that necessitate belief in them, and they also brought them the offering that fire consumes, yet despite that they denied them and killed them. This indicates that their disbelief was obstinacy, for they lied in their statement: ﴿"Indeed God has commanded us"﴾. ﴿And if they deny you﴾: this verse is a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ, by taking the example of others before him.

This indicates that their disbelief was obstinacy, for they lied in their statement: ﴿"Indeed God has commanded us"﴾. ﴿And if they deny you﴾: this verse is a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ, by taking the example of others before him.

ayyuh: I'll translate the passage now.

﴿Whoever is drawn away from the Fire﴾: that is, is removed and kept far away. ﴿You will surely be tested﴾: the verse is addressed to the Muslims. The trial in their persons is by death and illness, and in their wealth by calamities and spending. ﴿And you will surely hear﴾: its cause was the saying of the Jews, "God is poor," and their insults to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to the Muslims. ﴿You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: it refers to the Jews, to whom a covenant was taken concerning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), but they concealed it. It is general, covering everyone whom God has given knowledge. ﴿Those who rejoice in what they have brought﴾: the verse. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it was revealed concerning the People of the Book. The Prophet (ﷺ) asked them about something, and they concealed it from him and informed him of something else. They went out, having shown him that they had told him what he had asked them about, and they sought praise from him for this, and they rejoiced in what they had been given for their concealing from him what he had asked them. Saʿid al-Khudri said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites. When the Prophet (ﷺ) went out to a military campaign, they stayed behind from him and rejoiced in their sitting out, contrary to the Messenger of God. When the Prophet (ﷺ) returned, they made excuses to him and loved to be praised for what they had not done. ﴿So do not think them﴾: with the ta' and a fatha on the ba': it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ). With the ya' and a damma on the ba': the verb is ascribed to those who rejoice, meaning they do not think themselves safe from the punishment. Whoever reads "tahsabanna" with the ta' is addressing the Prophet (ﷺ), and "those who rejoice" is the direct object, and "in a place of safety" is the second object. The repetition of "fa-la tahsabannahum" is for emphasis. Whoever reads "la yahsabanna" with the ya' from below has deleted both objects, because the two objects of "la tahsabannahum" indicate them.

Here is the translation of the passage:

"And the alternation of the night and the day" (mentioned in al-Baqarah). "Standing, sitting, and lying on their sides" (﴿قِيَٰماً وَقُعُوداً وَعَلَىٰ جُنُوبِهِمْ﴾). That is, they remember Allah in every state. So these postures are a delimitation of the states of the children of Adam. It was also said: this refers to the prayer: they pray standing; if they are unable, they pray sitting; if they are unable, they pray lying on their sides. "Our Lord" (﴿رَبَّنَآ﴾). That is, they say: "Our Lord, You did not create this for no purpose; rather, You created it and created mankind, so that they would reflect upon it and thereby know You."

﴿We heard a caller﴾ — he is the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿Who calls to faith, "Believe in your Lord," so we believed﴾ — no, the text here reads: ﴿Our Lord, we heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord," and we believed﴾...

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 193–195:

﴿We heard a caller﴾ — he is the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿Who gave us promise upon Your messengers﴾, meaning: through the tongues of Your messengers. ﴿Whether male or female﴾ — min here is for explaining the kind; it is also said to be extra (zā'idah), since it follows a negation. ﴿Some of you are from others﴾ — women and men are equal in rewards and good deeds. ﴿And they were expelled from their homes﴾ — they are the emigrants (muhājirūn) whom the polytheists in Makkah harmed until they were driven out of it. ﴿A reward﴾ — in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 3, verses 196–198:

﴿Let not their movement through the land deceive you﴾ This verse is a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ). That is: do not think that the state of the disbelievers in this world is lasting, so that you grieve over it. The verb "yaghurranaka" is used with the meaning of "yahzunaka" (grieve you). ﴿A brief enjoyment﴾ That is, their turning about in the land is brief, when compared with what will escape them in the Hereafter. ﴿A lodging﴾ The word "nuzulan" is in the accusative, either as a circumstantial accusative (ḥal) referring to "gardens," or as a verbal noun (maṣdar). ﴿For those who are righteous (al-abrar)﴾ "Abrar" is the plural of "barr" and "barr," and its meaning is those who act with piety (al-birr), which is the ultimate point of taqwa (God-consciousness) and righteous action. Some of them said: "The abrar are those who harm no one."

[Qur'an 3:199] ﴿And indeed, among the People of the Book﴾ ... the verse. It is said that it was revealed concerning al-Najashi (the Negus), king of Abyssinia, for he was a Christian and then embraced Islam. It is also said that it was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Salam and others among the Jews who embraced Islam. ﴿who do not barter﴾ is a praise of them, and it contains an implicit rebuke of others who ﴿bartered the signs of Allah for a small price﴾. "Sabiru" means: endure against your enemy in battle. ﴿And stand guard﴾ means: station yourselves at the frontier posts (thughur) as those on garrison duty (murabitin), with your horses, prepared for jihad. It is also said that it means the ribat (spiritual vigilance; literally, garrison duty) of the servant between himself and Allah, that is, his pledge to perform obedience and abstain from disobedience. The first interpretation is more apparent. He (ﷺ) said: "A day of ribat in the way of Allah is better than a month of fasting and standing in prayer (qiyam) during it." As for his statement, "waiting for prayer, that is the ribat" (fa-dhalikumu al-ribat), it is a comparison to ribat in the way of Allah, due to the greatness of its reward. The murabit (one on ribat), according to the jurists (fuqaha'), is the one who resides in the frontier posts and stands guard there while it is not his homeland. As for those who live there permanently with their families and livelihoods, they are not murabitun, but they are defenders (hummah). This is related by Ibn Atiyya.
